div.head: WOMEN'S UHT.
div.p: WOMEN'S UHT.

A Great Sportswonian.—Lady Breadalbane is the author of a series of articles on sport and deer-stalking which will shortly be published in boek form. She is, with the Duchess of Bedford, considered one of the best lady shots in the country, many a Royal stag having fallen to her rifle. Lord and Lady Breadalbane spend the greater portion of the year at Taymouth Castle, their beautiful seat on Loch Tay, and for some time past Lady. Breadalbane has been seen very little in London. She is the youngest daughter of the late Duke of Montrose. Lord Breadalbane who has filled various offices in the Royal Household, received his marquisate at the instance of the late Mr. Gladstoneand in politics Lady •Breadalbane shares the Liberal opinions of her husband. In this she differs from her brother and nephew, the Duke of 'Montrose and Lord Graham, both of whem are Unionists. A Leading Hostess.—Lady Ilchester nee Lady Helen Stewart, only daughter of Lord and Lady Londonderry, whose hospitality during the present London season has been so greatly appreciated by the fortunate mortals bidden to partake of it, owns almost as splendid jewels as her mother-in-law, Mary Lady Ilchester, and among her most cherished and magnificent possessions is the necklace given her by her father on her marriage five years ago. The necklace is formed of flowers in emeralds and diamonds, strung together with diamond chains, an enormous emerald surrounded by brilliants forming a pendant. Lady Ilchester also owns some wonderful pearls,but nothing of course to compare with Mary Lady Ilchester's string of single black pearls, which was once the property of the ex-Empress Eugenie, and is said to have cost £30,000. Pearls, by the way, have two lustres, a grey and a green, the green however is said to be the most precious, and the pearls owned by Mary Lady Ilchester and Mary Duchess of Hamilton, possess this rare colouring. Stripes still Modish.—The tailors have become very clever in manipulating stripes, so clever indeed • that nothing in the way of trimmings is allowed by many of them for striped costumes. These shining lights rely entirely upon a clever arrangement of the material, but this requires such nice workmanship, that our tailor- made costumes are no less expensive even though a simple braiding is forbidden us. It is whispered that striped tweeds will be extremely fashionable for early autumn coats and skirts, and that blue and mole colour will be a leading combination. A Dainty Device.--The vogue for applications of flowers and scrolls in chintz and cretonne goes merrily on, and the idea has now extended to patterned or hand- painted chiffon trails and garlands being carefully' cut from such fabrics, appliqued to silk, gauze, ninon, muslin, and other similar materials. Sometimes the raw edges are oversewn, and outlined with darned silver thread, at others they are simply buttonholed over in floss silk, while a few models show the edges outlined with the very finest braid in a shade matching the deepest tone Of the design. The Greek Key Pattern.—The Greek ;ley-pattern is still greatly to the fore, even lace being disposed in this fashion. One of the most charming effects is how- ever gained by a somewhat Wide white cotton braid, arranged in this particular style, on white embroidered lawn and the home worker who has neither the time nor the inclination to trace and work out the pattern herself, will rejoice to hear that it can now be had in the shops ready-made. So far, only white and cream braids have made their appearance, but doubtless it will not be long before colours are available. How to Wash Silk Blouses.—When contemplating washing a silk blouse, the washer should choose a day when there is every probability of getting it through all the processes at top speed. The first thing to do is to make a lukewarm lather and wash the blouse in the ordinary way, then it should be rinsed through two lukewarm waters, and immediately hung in a breeze. While uniformly damp it should be taken in, as if it is allowed to become dry and then damped, it is all too liable when ironed, to look darker in some places than in others. Many people prefer not to bang tussore, Jap, and other thin silks, out in the air, but to roll them very tightly in a cloth for about half an hour, and perhaps this is the wiser plan. A moderately hot iron can be used for all silks, except crêpe de chine which should only be pressed with quite cool irons. The American t4irl.—America is noted for its wilder journalism, but the scheme adopted by one or two newspapers of giving a number of young women a "free trip "to Europe is an altogether admirable one. They are elected for this privilege by the votes of the readers. Those who get the greatest number of votes get the "free trip," and no one who met the girls from Ohio, who have been sight seeing in this country, and on the Continent would wonder at their success in such a com- petition. it is true -they have to hustle round pretty quickly to get through a long progromme in so short a time, but that is the American way, and the American girl combines a capacity for the enjoyment of sight- seeing with an untiring energy which makes her an ideal traveller. Her buoyanee of spirits is infectious and she is always a charming personality. Extravagances Lavished upon Pet Dogs.—The women who throng the fashionable dog shows, which are mostly held at this time of the year, may be divided into two classes—those who are real dog lovers, and those whose interest in animals has its origin in the Society craze for pets. Dogs are fashionable, and there are no limits to the extravagances which the Society woman lavishes 'upon her favourites. French women go to even greater lengths and there are establishments in Paris where every conceivable luxury for dogs, however grotesque, is supplied. There are toilet rooms, and show-rooms with dummy dogs dressed in morning, afternoon, and evening coats with jewelled collars and fittings, rubber shoes for rainy weather, and where such things as Russian leather travelling kennels, luxurious drawing-room lounging baskets may be obtained. There is a Dog Toilet Club in London, and here, many a fashionable pet is brought by the lordly footman to have its morning toilet attended to, before the carriage drive with its mistress. The aristocratic dog of the moment is the Pekingnese which boasts a pedigree of about two thousand years or more, but like all other fashions, that for canine pets changes, and first one breed and then another becomes all the rage in fashion- able Society. Slimness Fashionable.—Never perhaps has there been a time when slimness has been deemed so fashionable. This will proven bad bearing for those girls and women who suffer from an accumulation of adipose tisane, but they will be wise to refrain from anything approaching tight-lacing and drugs, courses likely to bring th3m to considerable grief. The woman who values her good health, will never touch drugs, unless prescribed by a doctor, and with regard to tight-lacing, such a pro- cedure not only causes imperfect circulation, palpitation of the heart, and other serious affections, but usually a red nose and a sallow skin. The too-abundant woman should simply avoid all food containing starch and sugar, she should also walk for at least two hours a day. and take as much physical exercise such as rowing, swimming, tennis, and bicycle riding as possible. Half an hour with the dumb-bells every morning before dressing will often accomplish wonders, and a course of massage is often successful when all other means have failed.

div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FAAH
PRINCESS AND DAIRYMAID:

An amusing incident occurred '‘ while the Prince and Princess of Wales were paying a visit to one of the working dairies on the occa- -sion of their recent visit to the Highland and Agricultural Society's Show in Edinburgh. The Princess admired and was about to lift a beauti- ful Marechal Niel rose from one of the tables, when a dairymaid hastily interposed, explaining that the rose was made of butter. The Princess expressed her admiration for the Work, and be- fore leaving shook hands with all the dairymaids.

div.head: FOR COOL WEATHER.
div.p: FOR COOL WEATHER.

A neat and useful costume for travelling or WO evenings at the seaside ,is shewn in our illu'.,tration. It is built of grey cashmere cloth striped with pale blue. The well-cut pleated skirt clears the ground all round, and is trimmed with two crossway bands of the material. The coat is semi-fitting, and is drawn in at the back with a crossway strap, which finishes in an up- turned point at each side of the loose-fitting fronts. The basque is pleated at the back, the fronts of the coat being finished with a narrow strapping of the material. The flat collat. is
'N

faced with pale blue cloth, and the three- quarter-length coat sleeves are finished with cuffs to match. With this costume is worn a pretty little hat of pale blue straw, trimmed with blue ribbon and a fancy white feather mount.

div.head: SOME SMART PARTY DRBSSES.
div.p: SOME SMART PARTY DRBSSES.

We are levelling in embroidery, and some of the most beautiful shades of crêpe-de-chine have inlets of lace round the skirt forming irregular points up and down; a similar trimming intro- duced on the bodice of a new form of coat, which fastens at the back, forms two points in front, has a short frilled sleeve and a round col- lar yoke of lace that is part and parcel of the high collar. Striped voile is exceedingly fashion- able, and this, too, is trimmed with lace inser- tions of a heavy make both on skirt and bodice. We are returning with much success to the old fashion of perpendicular bands of alternate lace and ribbon forming a plain flowing skirt and worn with a fanciful coat. These are various enough, but they all have one common feature, a conjunction with the kimono sleeve. Some have fanciful yokes and full fronts; most of them are loose, and discover a short all-round basque. There is more variety in fashion this year than we have ever seen. All styles are modish and all colours, but in nearly all there is an Empire disposition in the way the skirt is drawn up towards the middle of the back to meet a buckle or a bow. There is hardly any exception to the long drooping shoulder line, and the skirts with long, loose lines have at- tained the perfection of grace. The circular-. pleated skirts clearing the ground, worn with a three-quarter coat, are the *novelties of the moment in tailor-mades which put in an appear- ance at the most fashionable resorts. These modes are mannish. We look kindly on the cut- away coat, on the masculine waistcoat, on the high linen collar, often fastened with a hand- some stud, below which sometimes falls a jabot of lace.—Queen. _

div.head: BATHING COSTUME.
div.p: BATHING COSTUME.

As our holidays approach we are turning our attention to seaside attire. One of the most im- portant items is the smart little bathing cos- tume. An effective yet quite practical gown is depicted below, intended to be fashioned of fine blue serge, though it will be readily seen that it could be carried out equally well in other suit- able materials, such as galatea or bunting. The bodice fastens on the left shoulder with two

large buttons, and invisibly down the left side. The square yoke is composed of fine white serge. scalloped at the edges, and prettily embroidered with pale blue silk. The bodice is made wide ever the shoulders, and finished with short kimono sleeves of the white serge, which are also scalloped at the edge and worked with blue silk. The skirt is put on separately, and fastens down the left side, the hem being trimmed with a wide band of the embroidered white serge. THE NEATLY - DRESSED WOMAN. There is an exquisite charm about a neatly- dressed woman, says a weekly contemporary. She does not wear her hair_ loose,_ as if it is just

about to fall on her shoulders. Her gloves are not ripped at the seams, nor• are any buttons missing from her boots. Her veil does not reveal a hole over her chin, nor does the binding of her shirt shew ragged in places. Not many women shew their tidiness in these details, but

"Oh, I am—rather!" said Ralph with a laugh. "You'd better walk round with me," said Burchett. "Take a gun. The carrier can bring your bag. Mind that dog—she bites," he added, as they went out; and the dogs, which had been waiting outside, rose from their haunches with suspicious and angry growls. "Which, this one ? " said Ralph; and he stooped and laid his hand on the nozzle of the Irish terrier. She glared up at him for a moment with every hair on end like a wire; then, gradually, her anger died away, her brown eyes softened, and she thrust out her warm tongue and licked his hand.

"No, no! I've got to keep cool to-night." He smoked a cigarette with the same air of repression, but with a kind of patient impatience as if he were waiting for something; then, when half-au-hour had elapsed, he opened the door quietly, and crossing the small,- artistically decorated corridor, listened at Gibbon's door. The man was snoring. Talbot Denby came back to the dining-room, and unlocking a safe— an unusually large one—took out first a cash-box and then an old, long overcoat and a soft felt hat. From the cash-box he lifted a small bundle of notes and some gold. As he counted these, his lips grew tight nna his dark brows drew together with an anxious frown. He put the notes and the gold in hi pocket, replaced the cash-box in the safe, and put on the long coat and hat, turning up the collar of the former and pulling down the latter well over his face. As he assumed this disguise, his erect figure became bent, and, as if ineehanically and instinctively, he sleurl?,(l acre.,,s the room instead of walking wita hi,, wiur.l light and firm gait. As he let himself out of the flat stealthily, he listened once more at Gibbon's door. Striking across Lower Sloane-street he went quickly but sleachingly through the smaller and least frewnted of streets until he reached Soho, and, stepping before an ordinary-looking tobacco- nit,t's, which appeared to be closed like the rest of the shops in the squalid street, he knocked four times on the shutter.

The door was quickly but stealthily opened by an unseen hand, and Talbot Denby, going down the narrow passage, looking neither to the right nor left of him, as if h were familiar with the Fl. Ree, passed through a door into the usual kind of shop-parlour in which there was yet another (7.-lor. He gave the four knocks on this, and it was opened by a short, thick-necked, oily foreign Jew, with a villainous countenance which was rendered still more villainous by the smirk with which he welcomed his visitor.

"Goot efening, goot efening, Bare! " he said in a hoarse whisper—half servile, half impudent, and with a confidential leer which one would have thought would have been an irresistible temptation to the great Mr. Talbot Denby to strike him across his thick, evil lips. "I wash afraid you washn't coming; you wash so unlucky the other night. But there ! luck ish alwaysh changing; thatsh the beauty of it, thatsh what makes it so—what you call it ?—fashinating. Come thish way; there ish a goot company to-night." Looking straight before him, Talbot Denby followed the man into a low-ceilinged room,dimly lit by an evil-smelling paraffin lamp which hung from the ceiling, so that its Murky rays should fall upon a round table covered by a greasy green cloth, in the centre of which was a battered roulette board. _ _ _

Round the table were seated about a dozen men—a motley crew. There was the dissipated "gentleman" with bloodshot eyes and bags under them; the swarthy Pole with hollow cheeks and pointed chin adorned by a blue stubble; the well- to-do Jew merchant in evening dress, with a diamond stud in his creased shirt front and rings half way up the fingers of his dirty hands; the gilded "youth about town" with a vacuous smile on his flushed face; the bookmaker with red, swollen lips and bulbous eyes—in short, the usual crew of lost souls which may be found any night in their fitting place, the low gambling hells of London or Paris or Vienna.

They were so absorbed in watching the roulette board that they scarcely noticed the entrance of the new-comer and Isaacs, the keeper of the hell, who had to push two men apart so that he could place a chair for Mr. Talbot Denby. One of the men he bad displaced—the man on the right—gave a kind of snarl and muttered an oath as he looked up and sullenly shifted his chair. He was an evil-looking fellow—but so were they all—with shifty eyes and a cunning, cruel mouth which writhed as he blinked at the dancing ball on the roulette board. Talbot Denby scarcely glanced at him; and, taking his seat, at once fell into the attitude of the rest as he placed some gold on the table and pushed a sovereign into a black square of the design painted in circular form on the table. The baa fell to the corresponding colour, and he raked in his winnings with a curved white hand. As the played proceeded, and he won or lost, his stakes grew heavier' and some of the notes had taken their place beside the gold. There were many Filch piles in front of the players; it was astonishing that such a crew should be possessed of such wealth. - - -

For a time Talbot Denby's luck swung back- wards and forwards from good to bad, but presently the bad set in firmly, and one after another of the notes disappeared; but he played on, apparently unmoved, though his fellow gamblers might have seen, if they had not been too engrossed to notice, that his lips were grow- ing tighter and more bloodless, that his nostrils were sbecoming white and strained, and that the black eyes were glowing like points of fire under the half lowered lids.

There were but few of the notes left, and he was placing one of them on a red square, when suddenly his lips parted with a snarl like that of a dog his elbow crushed down upon the hand thp man beside him, and he turned on him with the fury of a wild beast; he had caught the man in the act of stealing one of the notes. The sudaen, low, repressed cry, all the more nartling for its repression, shook the other players from their absorption. Snatching up their money, they sprang to their feet as one nann, leaning forward and staring breathlessly at Talbot Denby, who had clutched the thief by the throat with an expression so savage' so primeval, in its malignant ferocity that it was, in its incongruity with the refined face and graceful form, simply appalling. The detected man struggled in the grasp of the low*, lean fingers which held him as if in a vice sathreatened to choke him; the two men were swiftly locked in a fierce embrace' and, swaying to and fro overthrew the table. There were no shouts; infleed, not a loud word was spoken, as if, even in that moment of intense strain and excitement, all were aware that they dared not inake any noise. Isaacs rushed towards them, waving and wring- ing his fat, dirty hands, and in a horse whisper imploring them to be quiet.

"Shentlemen, shentlemen ! "he hissed, hoarsely. "What ish the matter? Oh, Moses! The policesh —they'll hear you! What hal the matter Talbot Denby moistened his lips and turned his dry tongue in his mouth ere he could speak.

"This scoundrel has stolen a note from me!" he said, in a low voice. "It's a lie!" retorted the man, pawing at his throat and glaring at the white face above him with the air of a cur baulked of a bone.
"He has it in his hand now," said Talbot.

As be spoke ho bent towards a side table and, snatching up a spirit decanter, struck the man's fist a terrible blow. The man's hand opened and the crumpled note fell on the floor. He made a rush for his assailant, hut before he could reach him, the Jew had flung his arms round him and, aided by some of the other men, had dragged him to the floor. In springing back, the soft felt hat which had partly concealed Talbot Denby's face, fell off, !Ind he stood, the centre of the excited group, a strange contrast to the rest. He caught up the hat and put it on. The thief had got to his feet. but was still held by Isaacs and a couple of men.

"Out you go I," said Isaacs. "You're a scheat —a low scheat! We don't want your kindsh here. Thish ish a respectable place.'" As they pushed the man towards tlie door, he turned and looked over his shoulder and waved his bleeding hand at Talbot Denby. "See this!" he cried, hoarsely, as if he were still choking. "I'll make you pay for this some day. Pll make you sorry for it, swell as you are! I'll wait on you! It may be for months, it may be for years, but it may be to-morrow! I'll be even with you!" Talbot Denby, calm and cold again, regarded the man's working face and bloodshot eyes with haughty indifference, and turned away con- temptuously. He stood for a few minutes leaning against the wall, his arms folded, his eyes downcast. The table had been put on its legs again, play had been resumed as if nothing had happened. Isaacs came back presently., "He'sh quite gone, sare! " he said, stretching out his hands apologetically. "I'm shorry! I keen a respectable house. as vou know. sare." Talbot Denby waved his apologies aside End left the place. As he emerged into the cool air of the June morning, he drew a long breath through his closed teeth and shrugged lais shoulders. -
"My luck again!" he muttered. uI shall have to go to the Court, after all!" (Ts lit contitsuld.)

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

TANNERY TRIP.—On Saturday the Tannery Company gave their annual trip to the employes, the place chosen being Blackpool. At 7.15 a.m. on Saturday 300 of the employees and friends left Fiddlers Ferry en route for Blackpool, which was reached at 10 o'clock, the trippers each going their own way until 12 o'clock when 250 made their way to the Imperial Cafe, Bank Hey-street. Here Mr. J. B. Moston had made 'arrangements with Mr. Salthouse to provide dinner, which proved to be an excellent one. After dinner there were votes of thanks moved to the Company for their kindness; Mr. Moston being asked to convey the same to the Company on behalf of the employes. Leaving the Cafe, the visitors divided each for individual pleasure. Many were in favour of the attractions at the Tower and Winter Gardens; others going to South Shore, Morecambe and Fleetwood, and others taking advantage of the rowing and bathing facilities. The enthusiastic excur- sionists left Talbot-roacl Station at 8 p.ni on the return journey, arriving home at 10.20, all being %reed that a most enjoyable day had been spent.--Mr. Moston deserves much credit for the excellent manner in which he had arranged the day's programme. A PENKETH ATHLETE. —On Saturday the annual sports in connection with the Widnes Technical Schools were held at Widnes. A Penketh boy. T. Pennington,who is a scholar at the above named school, proved himself a promising athlete by bringing back to Penketh several prizes, his record being : first prize 100 yards handicap; second prize, 220 yards handicap ; second prize 120 yards invitation race; and first prize long jump; the distance he jumped was 15ft.11in. With- out doubt he is a promising athlete and we hope he will still follow up this notable performance.

ANGLER DROWNED. A young man named James Jackson, of Farnworth. Bolton, whilst fishing in a pond at Littlehulton, on Monday, was seized with an epileptic fit, and fell into the water and was drowned. His wife had vainly tried to dissuade him from fishing, but he insisted. The body was recovered by means of a fish hook by Police- Constable Kinghorn.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

_ At last Warrington occupy the proud position of }Anglers of the South-West Lancashire League. St. 'Helen.. who prior to Saturday were champions with an unboaton record have fallen before St. Helens Rees, and their defeat was partienlarly galling, as the Recs., ." Paper, is one of the weakest teams of the League. p„, l'ne result, of the meeting was a most Complete surprise, and sent the despised Rees on their way rejoicing. St. Helens were sot 83 to win, and ss they have of late shown a propensity for running up big scores, it. was generally expected that they would win. They had however, not reckoned with the bowling of Ratner. who took seven wickets for 17 runs, and con- tributed very greatly to their dismissal for 60. Warrington's fixture with Earlestown was set aside for Cresswell's benefit and was witnessed by the record crowd of the season. The Wsrrington professional is deservedly popular and everyone felt that that the Atomise of a handsome reward was fully merited. Warrington had first knock and made a disastrous start as with only two on the board Callon made a hard return to Broster. Wright is a favourite with the crowd and his appearance at the wicket was warmly welcomed. ' At first his play was rather restrained but after he had got his eye in he hit ont freely. Sikook was out to a foolish stroke,whilst Podmore threw his wicket n.sv for ~wo. -Connor announced his appearance by jumping out _to Bates and sending the ball over the boundary and as' nel ‘yriyht promptly followed suit the spectators were ighted with. the prospect of seeing some hard hitting. e°nnor however proved too venturesome and T-luish 11.1:met his sticks.

With four wickets down for under 40 Warrington's Position was none too rosy hut Bibby and Wright quickly altered the state of the game. Both hit out With the greatest freedom and the rate of scoring was nnusually rapid—in fact it was too hot to last. Wrif,ht became a little careless and was twice missed. With bis score at 77 he adjourned for a. little refreshment and two runs later was out. His innines had been of the breeziest description and whilst he was at the Wicket the score was carried to almost 150.

-- Bibby did not lnng survive and with his score at 45 'wea dismissed. The borne innings, however, did not end here as Cresswell commenced to bit ont and driving with great power qnickly ran rip 41 and carried the total to 204 when the closure was applied, Warrington having two wickets in band.

Crowther and Crawley 'opened with confidenre for Rarlestown and the first balls from both Cresswell and Callon were sent for four. Cre,sswell's first over was rather singular. The first bell Crowther clouted lustily whilst the next four deliveries completely beat the bet. Crowther lied a short life and when be had ten to his credit Cresswell found his wickets. Crawley played earefullybut could find no one to stay with him end at the close of the Forlestown innings which realized 84, Was not out with 39.

Cresswell was the most successful bowler of the after 110 on and kee,Ning a good length he bowled unchanged 'king six wickets for 35. At the close he took three okets in one maiden over dismissing Leigh and woolfe with successive deliveries and finding Bates' !,tumps with the last ball. Callon was hardly suited by '.'ne pitch and only claimed one victim for 35. Silcock lti two overs secured one for 8.

Warrington second put in a long spell of leather nonting on the Ea.rlestown ground and when they came to hat needed to score 206 to win. They however collapsed very badly and after a short opening stand by Hawtin and Thompson were tumbled out very rapidly with the result that their total only reached 55.

;Fames still continue to lead in the Warrington aril District Lnague but their record is hardly so ,good as that of Orford Barracks who with two matches fl hand are only three points behind. Cheshire Lines ligineers occupy second position but the probability 18 that before the close of the season they will have to taake way for others.

On Saturday the Engineers met Walkers Brewery Reid the regultant game was remarkable for low scoring. Batting first Brewery were unable to get going ad were all out for 26, Turner with 9 being top scorer. In response O.L.C. ran up 41 hut at the outset had a distinct fright as their opening men were got rid of very cheaply.

'iVilderspool Brewery have recently had a run of llisfortnne and on Saturday they again had to bow the 'Knee this time to Mackies. The printers did not run 'UP a very big score as their total was only 41, but this Droved too much for the brewers who were all out for 32. Had Hallows (15) found anyone to follow his AXltmple the result might have been different. As it was the next hignest score was seven by Briggs.

P. and K. (No. tIY came near to establishing a record for low scoring in their match with Walker's Brewery in the second round of the works competition on Tues. claY. The brewers batted first and with scores of over 20 by Dargan, Pearson and Cook, had registered 98 for 6 at the close of the 50 minutes play allowed. Norman then proceeded to give a display of fancy bowling and doing the bat trick, altogether took six wickets for three runs. Dargan was not far behind with four for ; and P. and K. were all out for 7, the grand total Including to extras 1.

Lovely-lane and St. James had a close fight on the Wilderspool-road ground on Saturday. Batting first Lovel"-lane were all out for 19 and then they proceeded to dismiss St. James for 15. Nine ducks were bagged during the afternoon and the highest individal score Was 6 not out by Plant.

Sankey Wire Mills on Saturday entertained Moore and Daresbury and proved too stong for them.. After an indifferent, start they ran up 85 Gleave (20) and hawthorn (16) being the principal scorers. Moore and bareshury could do nothing with the bowling of Cook and Gleave and were all out. for 32 Brough with 11 being the only one to reach double figures.

Out of a total of 46 for Latchford Baptists, Lester Claimed 24 and contributed in no small measure to the success of the team over Runcorn Highfield. Runcorn Icere all out for 25 and singularly enough more than half of the;r runs were credited to one player in the Person of Williamson.

Steps are being taken to form a League amongst the junior clubs of Warrington and district for next season. The idea is ah admirable one and should do much to encourage a love of the summer sport amongst the youngsters.. Enquiries should be addressed to Mr o . useph Bennett. 130, Battersby-lane, Warrington.
Same next week as this.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

To-day the Warrington Works Association send a team to meet, Eccbs in the return charity match and in consequence there will be no play locally. Last Satur- day a splendid afternoon's work was put in.the first and second rounds being concluded and the third got well in hand. To-day week the main will be finished and on the Saturday following the tournament for the teams will be resumed.

Cemetery second are going strong for the champion- thin of the Lancashire and Cheshire second team com- petition. On Saturday they figured with success in the semi-final, beating Drdsbury by 66 points. - Only one of their men Rosterne failed to win his game and he was defeated rather heavily. The team will have to meet Prestwich George in the final and are confident of success.
Crosfield's bowlers accomplished a remarkable per- formance on Saturday in scoring 480 out of a possible 481 against Orford Tannery the total points in their favour at the close of play being 178.
Members of St. Paul's Men's Bible Class on Saturday journeyed to St. Georges, Altrincham and were badly beaten in a match with the Church House team. Only four of their sixteen men won their games.

There was a good attendance at the Marquis of Granby on Saturday to witness a match between J. Hollinsworth and Tilley's novice. The men were very evenly matched, but Hollinsworth obtained a slight lead early on, which he managed to retain right to the end, finally winning by 34-41.

The moulders employed by Messrs. J. Smethurst and Son on Monday had a picnic to Stretton to celebrate the completion of the apprenticeship of one of their number. Here a main of bowls was played on the green attached to the Cat rnd Lion Inn. All the games were keenly contested, and some of the men showed con- siderable skill, notably R. Ward, who displayed great judgment.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Sr. THOMAS'S BAND OF lloPE.—The annual trip took place on Tuesday when the members together with a large number of parents and friends spent a very pleasant Iday at Southport. The party left the church gates at ;Bam, in two cars for the Central station where a special train was in waiting which soon landed them in Southport. Refreshments were served and the members !dispersed to enjoy themselves in their own way. The ;younger children spent most of their time paddling in 1 the water under the care of one of the workers who for I hours were sitting guard over a miscellaneous heap I of bats, boots,stockings,together with rook and toys for ; little friends at home, while the older ones lost no time lin transferring their coppers into the charge of donkey- drivers, boatmen and others, and swelled the crowd I round Punch and Judy and other shows. The parents I and friends found attractions in other ways—inspecting the latest fashions in Lord-street, drives in and out of ;town, or enjoying their first motor ride round the lake. One elderly lady, well known in the village, on being 1. challenged by some younger friends,went into the water chute. After tea Mr. Hallows said he was sorry the clergy were unable to be with them, but as they knew it wan from no lack of interest. He was pleased to have so ; many parents with them, and he hoped they would all use their influence with their friends and neighbours to , take an interest in the society, whose sole ' object was the welfare of young people.—Votes of thanks and cheers were given for the workers, 'of whom the following were present, assisting the superintendent in the management and comfort ;of the children, Mr. Caldwell. Mrs. Buckley, Miss Langley and Miss Hallows, Mr. Goodcliffe. As the ' children left the room for their last run on the sands a number of balls kindly given by Mr. L. Davies were • distributed amongst them and with these games of foot- ball and rounders was soon in full swing. Shortly after seven,but all torsoon, the return journey was com- menced, Warrington being reached at nine o'clock. , Transferred to the cars they were quickly landed back • at Victoria Square, the older friends tired out but the younger ones as fresh as ever, judging by their happy iveices, and wishing, they were setting off again. ! UNITED BAND o HOPE PICNIC.—The annual trip in ' connection with the Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope Society took place on Thursday ' when upwards of 150 members and friends visited Southport. The party were conveyed by bus to the Central Station journeying to Southport by special I train at 8.25. On arriving at their destination lunch '• was served at the Bath's Cafe, after which the party I quickly dispersed; availing themselves of the numerous • attractions of this charming holiday resort, the younger members indulging in the usual seaside pleasures of wading, donkey riding, sand digging, etc., whilst others • availed themselves of the charming drives, boating- on . the lake, water chute, etc. At 4.30 the party ' re-assembled at the Bath's Cafe where a substantial tea ; was served. After tea the evening was spent on the beach and lakes many visiting the various arcades and ; markets purchasing little mementoes of the day's onting.",The return journey was commenced at 9 o'clock, Stockton Heath being safely reached a little after ; 10 o'clock. all being thoroughly satisfied with the days outing. The arrangements for the comfort of the ' party, which were admirably parried out, reflected great ' credit on the Committee and also on the Secretary, Mr. G. Whitfield, to whose energy the success of the trip was largely due.

div.head: Farm Fire.
div.p: Farm Fire.

; Shortly before midnight on Sunday a fire broke out on the farm premises of Mr. William Weir, Lower : Walton, near Warrington. The Wilderspool brigade were summoned and under the command of Superin- tendent Cronghton were quickly on the scene. It was found that a stack of new-mown hay,containing about twenty-five tons was well alight. It was seen there , was no hope of saving the stack, 'and the firemen turned their attention to preventing the flames fre(in ; spreading to the adjoining buildings. In this their j efforts were successful. The fire, it is supposed, must have been caused by the lightning, and the damage. ; which is estimated at £lOO, is covered by insurance,

div.head: FREE FIGHT IN A LIFEBOAT.
div.p: FREE FIGHT IN A LIFEBOAT.

After the strike of Barrnouth lifeboat crew a year ago, occasioned by appointing a second coxswain of whom a portion of the crew disapproved, the lifeboat was on Wednesday launched for the first time by order of the inspector of the -institution. Soon after the boat was launched a man objected to the position of the coxswain. High words ensued, and a free fight followed in the boat, which was at.once turned shore- wards. A number of those aboard showed marks of fight.

You are strong—you will be able to swim," she said; "and you've got a life-belt too. Oh, it only had a life-belt I"

"You can have this one," Eveline said. The captain was not looking her way—an infirm old man claimed his attention. He thought that by this time the women had all been placed in the boats. Evellne took off the belt and irranged it round the poor creature's trembling form, then handed her forward and saw that she was placed safely in the boat. _ _

Why did she not then claim her own place? The boats were not crowded. She would not, as far as she knew, deprive anyone of a chance by leaving the ship. And yet she held back, some unconquerable reluctance assailing her, some extraordinary doubt as to whether her duty were done. Had ' everybody been brought on deck? There was a passenger on board, she knew, who had twisted his ankle badly at the first moment of the trip. He had remained in a private berth ever since, and nobody except the stewards seemed to have seen his face. She caught at the arm of a sailor and asked whether the lame passenger had been rescued, but• was pushed out of his path with an oath. A steward whom she encountered replied, frantically: "The ship's foundering! If the gentleman ain't in the boats already he'll be dead in twenty minutes. The water's in the saloon and the cabins aft. You'd better make haste yQurself, miss."

But she could not make haste until she was sure. As no one seemed inclined to go in search of the lame man she herself started out to discover him. That the expedition was a dangerous one hardly occurred to her. She felt that she could not leave a man to die like a drowning rat. His cabin had been very near her own; she might at least be able to help him up to the deck.

Down the compapion-way she ran, and along the saloon, which, as the steward had said, was already running with water. But she had not to go so far as the cabins. At the entrance to the passages beyond the saloon she saw lying the body of a man. She thought that he was dead, or at least insensible, and she hurried to his assistance. But he moved and looked up at her with a white, drawn face. He had dragged him- self from his berth and had almost fainted with the pain. _ _
"Jet me help you," she said. "You must try to make haste. The boats will be gone in a minute or two. Lean on me."
"It is no use. I had better stay where I am. You must go." "I came back for you. I will not go without you."
"You came back—for me ? You are—a brave —woman. But it is—too late."
He sank down again, as if incapable of moving forward. She was almost in despair.
"Crawl on your hands and knees," she said. "Don't give up. You are not brave if you give up so easily. I won't leave you. Let me help you if I can." _

Her words seemed to brace him. She could not see his face for the lights had gone out, but she felt that he was making an anguished effort in response to her appeal. He managed to crawl to the foot of the companion-way, and there he paused exhausted. The last orders were being given; there was a sound of oars sweeping the waters steadily; there was a cheer. "They have gone," said the man, in a steady voice. "For the love of Heaven let them see that you are here! Run up to the deck, they will come back to you. Never mind me." "I shall not desert you," said Eveline.

She ran up the steps and saw before her the burly figure of the captain, a sight which at first gave her confidence. Again she heard a cheer from the boats, and then she recognised the fact that the captain stood alone at the head of the gangway. He was looking at the boats and waving his hand. It was a sign of farewell.
Eveline dashed forward and laid her hand on his arm. "Is it too late ? she said.

The captain uttered a word which he did not often use, and gazed at her as if she were a very spirit of evil. "You here? And why did you not get into the boat at the proper time? Why, they have all gone! I'll call. Boat ahoy ! " He sent a tremendous shout over the side, and was answered by another fainter cry; but the sound of the oars still drew away from the ship. It was plain that the sailors were not willing to turn back.

"Too late!" mattered the captain, helplessly. He shouted agiin, but obtained no reply. A light fog seemed to have grown up 'round the ship since Eveline had been last on deck, and not a boat could be ,3 ee n . They had slipped quietly away while she had been urging the lame man to make a last fight for his life. "What does this mean, young lady ? " said the captain. "What are you doing here ? " "There is a lame man below who was for- go to " Eveline panted. "I remembered him, but nobody would help me. I ran down to warn him—he was in the saloon—he managed to get to the foot of the steps. I don't think he can get any further without help---" The captain glanced at her and strode back to the companion-way. "Friend of yours ? " he asked, as he swung himself down the steps. "Oh, no; I don't know his name."
"So you've sacrificed yourself to a perfect stranger! I saw you just after that crazy woman—. I thought you went with her. Didn't I see you with a life-belt 2"

"The poor woman wanted it more than did. I can swim, if necessary," said Evelinc. "H'm ! " The captain's tone was grim. "You may be sorry,yet that you let it go. Here's your , protege, fallen in a dead faint apparently. I'll 'do my best to get him up to the deck. But if the boat should begin to roll-" He did not conclude his sentence, and Eveline gathered that he rather feared that the Iris had but a few minutes longer in which to live. She was being gradually swamped, and would probably fall into deep water and be lost, together with the three human beings left on , board. 1 There was a pause while the girl waited, listen- ing until the heavy steps of the captain were again heard as he scrambled up the stair with a I very heavy burden in his arms. He laid the insensible man down on the boards of the deck, and went away in search of a stimulant if any could yet be procured. He was some minutes in. finding a bottle of brandy; but in his absence Ev'eline bathed the man's forehead with cold water until he opened his eyo;.' Then he smiled slightly and said one word. -; "Eveline ! "

She had not seen his face before. Now a gleam of .starlight enlightened her. It was the face of Philip Thurston, a man whom she had once driven away from her, although she loved him as well as her heart knew how. She uttered a little gasp, a little sob, and started back.

"It can't be—Philip ! '' she said, slowly. "Yes, Philip. You saved my life, Eveline." "Only—for a little time," she said, hoarsely.' "Is it so bad? Is the boat going down?" "I'm afraid so. Here is the captain; we will ask him."
The captain_ administered the brandy, but

wotia'Ainswer no questions nennizeu. "I can't say.' 'We're in the hands of Provi- dence," he remarked. "It's just possible that if the tide has reached its height and is beginning to go down—which I think is the case—we might be left high and dry, stranded for a few hours, but safe. Then, if they send out boats to rescue us, we might get off. But it's only a chance. We may be in Eternity in another quarter of an hour, you know. Diq you feel the boat rock just then? If it topples over, we're gone." He walked away and paced the quarter-deck in his old manner, but without going very far. Evell'ne drew nearer to the man whom she had once loved, and pillowed his head on her knee. "So you have not quite forgotten me ? " “No. "You are not married ? " "Oh, no, no! Philip ? " "Don't think so meanly of me, Eveline. Don't you know that I loved you and only you! I shall never care for any other woman, although you treated me like a dog." She was silent; but his words, roughly spoken as they were, thrilled her with delight. He loved her still! "You are in just the same position, I suppose," he went on—"you are rich still ?" "Yes, lam rich. My father is dead. He made me a rich woman." "And you live in Grosvenor-square, I suppose? Well, it was a beautiful house—l remember it well. And you have the place in Hertfordshire too? lam glad you have 01 the things you loved so well." "Philip, Philip—don't be so hard on me!" she said.
. . . Are you married,

on you? How's that? You told me very plainly what your wishes and intentions were when last I saw you. I refused your wealth—you refused to share my poverty. You loved riches, luxury, pleasure—you refused to thifik- that you had any duty to your neighbour or yourself. Is not that true? We are in the presence of death—tell me, is it not true ? " "It is perfectly true," she said, in a faint voice.

"I am glad you acknowledge it. You were never slow in acknowledging the truth, even when it was most damaging to yourself. I never knew whether that was a virtue or a vice of yours." "A vice," she answered. "I used to be brutal in those days." "Brutal is an odd word to apply to such a dainty lady," he said; and she felt that his eyes gleamed at her in the semi-darkness. But she found it absolutely impossible to defend herself. She tried to minister a little to his comfort. She called- the captain to look at his injured foot, • and together they devised means of easing.the , pain a little; but when all was done that could ' be done, she took her seat again beside him and drew his head upon her knee. "Is that comfortable?" "Yes.' but you will be cramped." "Not at all. I don't mind." "Miss Graham is impervious to fear and fatigue where other people's welfare is concerned," said the captain, stopping abruptly before the pair. "If we ever get safe, to land I shall let all the , country know how pluckily she has behaved. She must \have saved the lives of a dozen women and girls—possibly, sir, she has saved yours too." Then he turned and resumed his dreary pacing of the deck. "Is that tali() ? " said Philip, with his eyes on her face. "The captain exaggerates. I helped some of the poor women a little," she said, softly. "Any- one would have done the same." "Would you have done it in the old days ? " She meditated for a moment or two, then replied, with the frankness that he had already noted in her: "No,I don't suppose I should. I was too fond of my own comfort. I thought myself too important to be useful. to other people." "And you have changed?" There was a note of wonder in his voice. "If I have not, changed," said Eveline, looking away from him, "I could almost hope that wa should go down into the sea to-night." There was a silence, broken only by the lapping • of the water against the sides of the vessel. Even that seemed softer to Eveline's ear, and she , fancied that the slight rocking sensation of which she had been conscious had almost ceased. As she listened and doubted a little the captain came , up to her hurriedly, with a gleam of hope in his honest face. , "I'm sure of it," he said, triumphantly. "The tide's changed. It's going out, and we are here still. She'll last till the next high tide; but no longer. Heaven grant they send the boats to take us off! I should think they are sure to come

back." "If they come, when will they reach us?" "Oh, by six o'clock, I hope. If they are much later, they'll be too late' that's all. It's only six miles to Alderney—if they don't miss their way in the fog." "It is only a chance," said Philip, slowly. "I suppose you are sorry. As for myself, lam rather relieved to think of leaving the old earth so soon." "I feel as you do," said Eveline. sorry either. Except for one thing." "What is that ? " "I had just begun some work that I wanted to carry out." "Work? You ? " There was a certain irony in his tone. If she noted it he could not be sure; for she answered with perfect calm: . "I have been a nurse in a hospital for the last two years. I have now begun to build a cottage hospital for children in my own grounds. I meant to be the first matron and superintendent Children interest me," she said, rather lamely; "and as I am qualified, and have nothing else to do, I thought I would make an experiment." "You ? " he said again. "And why not I? Because I was a silly, cold- hearted girl when I parted from you, is it not possible that I should have my eyes opened to my mistake, and should try to love my fellow- creatures and help them a little bit? You are unfair to me." "I beg your pardon," he said, composedly. "But it seems that you are not—not the Eveline I.used to know." ‘"Yes, the real Eveline—the one that I tried to conceal." "What changed you?" "I don't know that I can tell you that." "Not even now when it may be our last hour together ? " She was silent for a few minutes, looking out with troubled eyes upon the sea. "Tell me," he whispered, brokenly. "I changed," she said, very slowly, "when I found out that I was like other women—that I could love, and that I had sent away from me the only man--" She paused ; she could not complete her sentence. "Oh! tell me, Eveline, who was that man— the man you loved?" "Do you not know, Philip? Can you not guess? And by my own pain I learnt to measure the pain of others. That was all." "You loved me—all the while ? " "Yes." "Then, Eveline, if we live—my darling--" "Ah we shall not live," she cried, "and that why I tell you. I could not die, Philip, Ofthout letting you know that I love you with all my heart and soul.' "Let death come when it likes, then," Said Philip, valiantly, "for it finds us together; and we shall never be separated any more. I%ly darling, you shall be mine indeed—in life and death." So for a time they sat, hand in hand, close indeed to death, but full of a strange happiness. And when dawn shewed itself over their heads they heard in the distance the lapping of the oars as the boats returned, and they knew that they had Life to meet—not Death. Out of the heart of danger they had plucked love and happi- ness, and even, they hoped, an eternity of bliss! [THE END.]

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] BETWEEN LIFE AND DEATH
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] BETWEEN LIFE AND DEATH
BY ADELINE SERGEANT,
Author of "A Story of a Penitent Soul," "Beyond I Recall," "Seventy Times Seven," "In Vallain- ! brosa," "Out of Due Season," &c.

On the night when the Iris, a crowded pleasure- boat, struck the dangerous rocks known as the Casquets, off Alderney, and was almost dashed to pieces before morning, there was at least one of her passengers who would have maintained that for her death had no particular terrors. She did not expect it, for she was young and strong; but it was her firm conviction that if it were offered to her and she could 'accept it without wrong-doing, she would. For, in her own opinion, she had lost all that makes life worth having, and the road that stretched before her was grey and uninteresting. And the worst of it was that she herself had helped to make it so. But she had got past the period of self-reproach. She had lost interest even in herself and her own doings—and interest in oneself is usually the last thing that disappears.

Certainly Miss Eveline Graham did not present a disconsolate aspect to the world at large. She was a girl of striking appearance: tall, slender, yet vigorous-looking, with clearly-cut features and a pale skin; large grey eyes fringed with long, curling dark lashes; dark, ruffled masses of hair, standing up from her broad brows and sweeping back in great loose waves to the nape of her neck, where it made a splendid knot of blackness. The expression of her face was sweet, yet listless in its sweetness; but the lines of her mouth spoke of decision, as though there were a hidden store of strength behind sweetness and listlessness alike. She was well-dressed, with a sealskin coat to wear when the wind blew chill which was the envy of every other woman on board. She had never known what it was to stint herself; she had been rich from the day of her birth, and it was no wonder that in the course of her five-and-twenty years of life she had some- times been called selfish and heartless and cold.

The Iris had landed a few persons at Alderney and Guernsey, and had taken others on board but for the most part the passengers were folks "on pleasure bent," who had come out for a few hours' cruise. It was understood that they would reach the English coast that night, unless the boat's course were delayed by fog or storm. Experienced mariners watched with some dismay the appearance of a slight sea-fog. But at first it did not seem as though it were likely to be dangerous. It thickened a little as daylight waned; but few of the passengers, ensconced in a brightly-lighted saloon' knew much about it, and after a well-served dinner they held an impromptu concert, at which the great feature was the singing of comic songs by a music-hall star. Eveline sat slightly apart from the rest of the audience and listened quietly. There was not any expression of distaste or condemnation upon her face; but the music-hall singer was rather nonplussed by her attitude—her thoughts seemed so very far away. And, indeed, she failed to remark whether it was "mother" or "father" who, after all, "laid the carpet on the stair," for she was thinking of the past and what might have been if she had once shewn herself a great-hearted woman, and whether it was even possible to retrieve the past. Thus, when a sudden crash was heard, and a tearing noise, and a strange whirr of machinery —and then a sudden silence, strange and awful, with only the lapping of waves against the ship's side to be heard—it was less of a shock to Eveline Graham than to any of the startled men and women who had been laughing unrestrainedly at the song a moment before. "No danger! Compose yourselves, ladies and gentlemen ! " an officer's voice rang out. "A trifling damage to the machinery, that is all. We shall be off again directly." • "I suppose we have struck the Casquets," said one of the passengers, a man who was decidedly too well-informed. "Off again! So we may be, but to the bottom of the sea."

A wail followed his hasty words; women burst into tears, and men groaned aloud. The officer wrathfully bade the speaker hold his tongue; but it was not easy to silence the questions which assailed.him on every side. There were strange noises from without—the creak and grind of timbers, the rushing of the sea. The passengers crowded towards the com- panion-way, but at the top of the steps the captain met them, very pale, very stern, and with some- thing in his hip-pocket which he grasped very firmly as he spoke. "I am sorry to say, ladies and gentlemen, that the boat has had a Slight mishap. The fog has landed us on the edge of a sunken rock, and I'm afraid we shall not get off _till morning. But the sea is calm enough, and the fog's lifting, so I propose to launch the boats and take the passengers back to St. Anne's." An immediate outcry succeeded his words. Some of the passengers shouted that they would stick to the ship, others that they \ would not venture their lives in open boats on the sea; but the majority tried to make a rush for the deck, and the captain had to shew his revolver and threaten drastic measures unless his orders were obeyed. The passengers were to range themselves on the deck certainly, but in good order. The women and children were to take possession of the boats, and the men were .to follow them. And when the first few moments of panic were over the frightened crowd obeyed the captain, and each man played his part gallantly. Naturally the women were more difficult to manage than the men. They shrieked and sobbed in turn. Eveline did her best to soothe some of them, and her calmness brought comfort to their spirits. She found herself the centre of a little crowd of girls, women, and children, all listening to her, clinging to her, begging her to save them. She smiled a little as she heard their wild words, and she bade them be of good cheer. A young officer came up to her at last, and even in that hour did not forget to touch his cap. He had a great admiration for Miss Graham. "We shall haie to give you a testimonial for taking such good care of the children," he said to her, with a smile. "You must make ready, it will be your turn soon. I've brought you a life- belt; it will help you if there is any mishap." "You think it will be a dangerous matter to get to land ? " "We may do it," the young man said, with a shrug, "if the fog lifts. But to me it seems inclined to close in again." They were out of hearing of the women and children, or else lie would not have spoken so Eveline turned her grave grey eyes upon
'"And what about the ship? Would it not bfi better to remain on board?"

"The old Iris? Oh, she'll go to bits before morning. The boats are not very safe, but they are better than this tub, which is a wreck already. So we must do our best to save the passengers." -"We must indeed," said Eveline, as if her ,heart rose to the task. "Thank you for telling me, Mr. Severn'e."

"I hope you don't mind. You do not look as • if you were easily frightened," said the young man. "I thought you would like to know the truth—it's for your hearing only. Now then, forward women and childred. One by one, please! " "Oh, I can't !—I can't!" cried one young girl, as she east an eye at the boat rocking backwards and forwards on the dark water, which seemed so unaccountably near. "We shall be drowned— I know we shall ! "

"Go forward, dear," said Eveline's calm voice in her ear. "It is quite a short run to Alderney, I and you will be safe enough in that big boat. Don't be afraid." And the girl shuddered but 1, passed on. Another woman was in tears. She had two : children with her, and could not carry both of I them. It was with difficulty that Eveline per- suaded her to commit one of the children to the arms of an pfficer to be handed down to the sailors; but she was successful at. last. "I don't know what we should have &Ire with- out you," the young third officer found time to Whisper in her ear. Then he was gone, for his duties took him to the other side of the boat. Two women only temained—Eveline and a small, middle-aged, nysterical person, who was lying in a heap on the deck, and whom the captain threatened to hand over the thwarts like a bundle if she did not speedily bestir herself. "I shall be drowned ! " cried the scared creature, in a quavering undertone. "I'm so weak --I shall not live through it." She opened her eves at Eveline. with s.t.Tue horror in their depths.

div.head: DEATH AT THE WICKETS.
div.p: DEATH AT THE WICKETS.

On Monday at Wakefield an inquest was held concern- ng the death of Ernest Sugden, aged 46. The jury found the cause to be heart failure, from excitement and over-exertion. While playing cricket on Saturday Sugden bent over his bat and fell forward on his face and when the umpire went to him he was already dead
CREWE MURDERER MURDERER REPRIEVED.

Mr. Feßhein, the solicitor acting on behalf of the boy Thomas Parrett, who was sentenced to death at Chester Assizes for the murder of a fellow-workman, near Crewe, on Tuesdar received a notification from the Home Secretary, to the effect that he had advised his Majesty to commute the capital sentence to one of penal servitude for life. It was thought frow the first that the boy who is only 17 years old, would not pay the full penalty of,his crime.

div.head: NEW MAGAZINES.
div.p: NEW MAGAZINES.
FRY'S MAGAZINE.

" Fry's Magazine" for August appears with a very attractive holiday-looking cover—a mixed bathing scene —and the interior fulfils the promise of the exterior. Mr. E. H. D. Sewell writes intimately of the various members of the South African cricket team,all of whom are happily portrayed by Charles Ambrose. Another cricketer, Mr. D. L. A. Jephson, recently captain of Surrey, contributes a dramatic cricket story. "Favourite Strokes of the Leading Lawn Tennis Players " are described, and very ably explained by Mr. Eust!ice E. White. Mr. Montague A. Holbeiii, who is now thinking of repeating his attempt. to swim across the Channel. has a most interesting article on 'Problems of the Channel Swim." Miss Maud F. Drummond, the ex-lady champion croquet player of England, writes on some of the intricate points connected with croquet. Golf players will find plenty in the magazine to interest them. There is an article on putting strokes, by last year's open champion, James Braid; a most instructive and useful account of the various golfing centres suitable for holiday visits, with hints as to fees, and travelling and hotel expenses; and there is a symposium by a number of well-known golf players who ari noted for long driving, explaining what they believe to be the secrets of tlifdr success in that direction. Motorists will read with interest the amusing account, by Owen Llewellyn, of a tour in Spain, profusely illustrated by the well-known" Punch "artist, L. Raven Hill.

div.head: TIPS TO SEA-BATHERS.
div.p: TIPS TO SEA-BATHERS.

----• The August number of the "Captain "the hundred- and-first issue of this magazine for boys and and" old boys," is atypical holiday number—brimful of excellent fiction and seasouable articles. Amongst the former are included lengthy insfalments of two popular serials —" The Fatal List,' a story of the French-Revolution, by Herbert Hayens ' • and Jackson Junior," a public school cricket story, by P. G. Wodehouse—and five first- rate short stories—school, adventure, and humour—viz., "A Problem in Mathcmaticst he story of a scholarship, "At the Eleventh Hour," a tale of a boy and a burglar; "His Old Ship," a fine sea yarn; "Miss Heapy," a story of a seaside hoax; and "Bill Bailey," a University boating story. "Sea-Bathing in the Summer Holidays," is an eminently practical article by , F. G, Aflalo, full of useful tips and suggestions; "The Birds of the Orkneys" is a chatty paper on the feathered visitors to these northerly islands; 'Do animals laugh and Cry ?" is a study of sympathies and feelings of our dumb friends; and " Tbe Sunnyside ' Schoolboy " affords a picture of the young Boer at school. There are in addition the usual Corners "devoted to photo- graphy, philately natural history, chess etc., and in his editorial chat the" Old Fag" descants on the sub- ject of early rising. There are, too, competitions, in which cameras, cricket bats, fishing roes, and other useful articles are offered as prizes. Altogether an admirable number.

THE WIDE WORLD MAGAZINE. The August" Wide World "is so full of good things that it is difficult to select articles for special mention Perhaps the most important narrative is "Selling the Empire's Secrets," a British soldier's strange story of his dealings with a foreign spy who wanted to obtain plans and photographs of a fortress. This unusual story is commended to the earnest attention of the public and the military authorities. Another remark- contribution is "An Alligator Hunt ,by Night," describing what the author terms" the most hazardous and thrilling sport on earth." "Fighting a Burning Gaswell," illustrated by some unique photograps, will rivet the readers attention ; while Six Thousand Miles on Horseback," the world's record long-distance ride, is a fascinatinr, account of a magnificent accom- plishment. In "The Romance of mining" we have a number of stories contributed by prospectors and others showing how largely the element of luck enters into the miner's life. Half a score of other articles and stories, all of an out-of-the-ordinary nature, go to com- plete an excellent issue.

THE BOULOGNE BOAT. A shrill whistle, and the Quay begins to wake up. The douciniers adjust their belts, pull their caps forward, and resume their stiff official attitudes. Their old lady colleague folds her knitting neatly, and stores it in one of the capacious pockets of her blue apron. Benevo- lence at once deserts her features, and the lynx eyes gleam -shrewder than ever. These officials have nothing to do with the Paris train which will- soon be coming in; we of England, when outward bound, are their only prey, but it would not do for the authorities to be seen in d‘shabill4. The porters stretch them- selves, kicking the dogs as they do 50..; the dogs howl, the porters swear, the quay is alive again. As soon as we hear the whistle announcing the train, we on board, moved by that love for our neighbours which is uppermost in every Christian's soul, hasten to secure all the deck chairs, cramming the superfluous ones with bags and wraps lest the belated traveller should find a corner to lay his weary bones on. Then comes the rumble of a crowd talking all at once. The French element is uppermost in the train contingent. In the crush families have been separated, and the anxious voices of mother and paterfamilias are heard on all sides: Marie, where art thou, my child? Albert ! Jean ! " When the lost one is found,anxiety gives place to irritation and a smart slap on the face is the truant's reward. A Frenchman, tres-snob, in full nautical costume dernier eri, approaches. His keen eyes have detected two inches of spare wall by us. Monsieur takes off his admiral's cap with a flourish,and explains in his equisite French manner that it is Madame's first sea journey in fact, with a conscious smile, "it is Madame's first journey without her mother." We nod sympathetically, congratulation written large on our countenance. Monsieur bows anew, Madame appears; we Jump up at sight of her, and make ample room for her deck chair. Monsieur disappears, to come back one moment later followed by two sailors loaded with beribboned muslin cushions, bat-boxes, flowers, etc. Monsieur gives us another sweep of his cap; Madame,, another languid and imploring smile; and we move still farther away to make room for the luggage. Monsieur murmurs audibly his approbation of the " entente cordiale," and is loud in his praise of " ces gentilshommes anglais " ; we feel most uncomfortable. The boat is loaded, the luggage all safely on board. A bell is rung, the French porters, after a great many shrugs of the shoulders, a great deal of hustling and puffing and blowing, depart, the gangway is removed the boat whistles we are off. On our way seaward, we cross two large fishing boats being rowed home by their crews. And so we say good-bye to the quaint old town and its good-humoured, hard-working population. By the time we leave the harbour, Madame has des- patched a plate of sandwiches, more chocolates, some fruit, and sundry delicate "bonbons." She is getting deadly pale. Monsieur rushes up to her, offers his arm —they vanish. We do not see Madame again until we reach Folkestone.---Maurice Berenger, in the August (Summer) Number of the "Pall Mall Magazine."

div.head: NEY AND THE OLD GRENADIER.
div.p: NEY AND THE OLD GRENADIER.

When he entered Ney's room in order to read to him the letter containing the instructions as to the several persons with whom he was permitted to have inter- views, he found him guarded by two grenadiers i cheval of the Royal Guard. After the letter was read, the Marshal said, "I will first confer with my notary, then I will see my wife and children; as to a confessor, let them leave me at peace; I have no need of the priest- hood." At these last words, one of the veteran grena- diers, standing at attention, said, "You are wrong, Marshal." and, pointing to his arm, ornamented with several chevrons, "I am not as illustrious as you, but I also am an old soldier. Well, never have I gone so boldly under fire, as when I have first recommended my soul to God." These few words, prottounced by the gigantic grenadier in an agitated and solemn tone appeared to make a strong impression on the Marshal. He went up to the old soldier, and, patting him on the shoulder, said with emotion," Perhaps, won brave, you are right; you give good counsel." He then inquired, " What priest can I summon ?" and, being told that the Luxembourg was in the parish of St. Sulpice, of which the cure, l'abbe de Pierre, was very highly thought of said "Beg him to come to me. I will receive him after my wife." The grenadier's advice had borne the desired fruit.—From "Deaths of the Marshasl " in tbo " Cornhill Magazine" for August.

The deposition of the THE KOREAN EMPEROR or KOREA by the CRISIS. Japanese is a step forward in the policy adopted by the victors in the Russo-Japanese struggle of providing the Island Empire with the necessary outlet for her superfluous population. Japan has looked upon Korea as her natural direction for extension for many years. Japanese and Koreans have never been good friends. Time after time attempts have been made to conquer the Hermit Kingdom. Centuries ago Korea was backed up by China, and the Japanese found the task of subjugation rather more than they could manage; but the Koreans have never been a strong military ' people, and the gradual advance of Russia, coro-; bined with the decline of Chinese power, has been their undoing. It is not a profitable task:to corn pare the professions of individuals or of nations with their performances. History shows in too many cases that the real objects of wars have been obscured only to be revealed later on, when the ability to carry out those objects has been established. That Japan was fighting for the indepence of Korea in the late war was a fiction which may have deceived some people. To them no doubt, it will be a source of disagreeable sur- prise that victory has meant not independence for Korea, but a condition of subjection in which she was not while Russian influence remained supreme. With the abdication of Ll Hsi the last vestige of Korean independence has disappeared. The Ex-EmPERok had ruled his people with much good intention if not with overwhelming success. But against the forces of Russia on the one hand and Japan on the other, he and his peaceable subjects had very little chance. Of the true object of Japan it is not necessary to speak with undue;harehness. The Government at Tokio has a difficult problem to lace, Japan,

with all her success, as a result of the wisdom of the Mikado in accepting Western civilisation, suffers from restriction of commercial opportunity. Her two great wars have been undertaken, whabr ever the professions of the Governments may have been, for the purpose of securing markets for her goods. That is not an unrighteous ambition, and, to some extent, it has been justified both in Formosa and Korea. Of the latter case, however much natural sympathy may go with the weaker, it is yet too early to pass judg- ment upon Japanese dealings. Oriental ideas differ very greatly from those which obtain in the Wester' hemisphere, and our own standards of international conduct and policy may not perhaps be justly applied to the process adopted towards , the Koreans. One consideration which it is not 1 ; possible to ignore in reviewing the situation is the necessity which the Japanese Government must feel for strengthening their hold upon Korea at as early a date as possible. To drive the Russians out was no small task, but to establish the Japanese as the acknowledged masters of that section of easternmost Asia is a still greater. The problem is not merely commercial; it is also military, and upon its solution rests the national future of the Japanese Empire. The practical effect 1 of the deposition of Li Hsi is to place the Govern- ' ment of Korea entirely in the hands of the Marquis ITo, one of the most sagacious of the Mikado's advisers, who will now, to all practical purposes,be 1 the dictator of the future of the Hermit Kingdom. His object will no doubt be to place a harrier as strong as possible against Russia in Korea. What- ever the feelings of European nations regarding the morality of the Japanese action, the material benefits which will accrue t-., Korea by reason of the substitution of an up-to-date administration, animated by the spirit which has made Japan herself so powerful, cannot be ignored, and for the comfort of Diropean nations it may be asserted that Japan will not, whatever her desires may be, be able to keep the whole of the commercial advantage for which she has worked to herself.

The half-yearly meeting of PARR'S BANK, LTD. Parr's Bank, Limited, is always an event of much local interest, apart from the fact that the meeting is held in the town, because this great banking cncern was founded in Warrington, which witur- ally takes a pardonable pride in the great success which has attended the operations of the company. Then, too, the speech of Mr. Cecil F. Parr, the chairman, is looked forward to each year for the reason that it is far from being a dry-as-dust state- ment of facts and figures, but instead surveys the nation's commerce and prosperity in a broad- minded and informative fashion. The company has, once again, the pleasure of looking back upon a period of very successful trading, for the available profits on the half year amount to no less than £340,41 which provides a dividend at the rate of 19 per cent. per annum—and admits o considerable addition to reserve and other funds Mr. Parr, on Thursday, hardly covered so wide a field in his remarks as on previous occasions, but he alluded to one very interesting topic— that of consols, which have created some concern in the minds of investors for a considerable time. Mr. Parr answered the question " Why are consols so low ? " by pointing out that in addition to the influence of political disturbances and unrest abroad,the public was not investing in consols to the same extent. They were no longer con- tent with a 3 per cent, return, and the discovery of. safe and remunerative invest- ments elsewhere had effected the price of" gilt- edged securities." This was a simple reason, which the speaker thought had been largely over- looked. He voiced no concern whatever at the fluctuations of consols, and the investing public may, apparently, rest assured that the stability of the country is not "going to the dogs " just yet. Trade is good, and the chairman of" Parr's sees many signs of it continuing good for sometime yet. While the banking trade continues so pro- fitable, there is evidently no shortage of cash in the country. We hope that the present era of prosperity may be a long one!
We have always realised TEM SMOKE that the smoke nuisance is NUISANCE. a real 0'63, and that it con-

_ stitutes 'a menace and danger to public-health, but unfortunately the local authority, almost to a man, scoffs at the idea that the smoke does any harm. With the exception of Alderman Bennett, no one ever raises a voice in the Council Chamber against the evils which pour forth thick and black from our factory and workshop chimneys. The Alderman has long been both general and army of the crusade against the smoke nuisance, and recruits are slow in com- ing to the flag. But apparently, if apathy and contempt reign supreme in the Borough Council, there are people in the town who can and do realize the harm that the smoke is daily doing. A week ago, we published a letter from an "ex-Warrington house- wife "who rejoiced that she had at last got away from the polluted atmosphere of the town to the clean, health-giving air of the country. This week we publish letters from two ladies who are still Warrington housewives, and they both bemoan the gloom and dirtiness of their surroundings &al- sequent on the smoke which "thronged the air and darkened Heaven," rind envy the lady who is an ex Warrington housewife. The wives realise the hardships of town life, if their husbands don't, and they are convinced by sad experience that • , much of the cleaning and washing which make 1 nousework a drudge might be made unnecessary by checking smoke pollution. If the women will only tackle the smoke nuisance they will soon set the men thinking. It is some satisfaction to know that the fight against the smoke is gaining strength all over the country. Warrington is one of the backward and unenlightened tewns. We note that the question is to come before the forth- coming conference of Chambers of Commerce in Liverpool, where a resolution will be introduced advocating reform in fuel consumption and recog- nising a clear atmosphere as "a desirable consummation." Legal remedies of a more stringent character are suggested,but probably no real advance will be made till we get government inspection in the place of the half-hearted local supervision.

One of the things for which A FIELD FOR our American cousins are INVENTIVE Gmvus. distinguished is th 9 fresh- ness end virility of the new words which they coin. The inhabitants of a new town " out West,'' in their admiration for President Roosevelt, have christened it "Teddy- yule." We are anxious to give our readers some idea of the charming results which would follow the adoption of this method of naming new places here. When the King opened the new street made by the L.C.C., they might have called it "Teddy's Way," while Aldwych might have been called Johnny- street, after Mr. John Burns. Judging ny what has appeared in some London papers recently, "Dickey's Meadow" would not be a bad name for theAldwych site, seeing that the difficulty of letting it—whether it be the fault of the present Council or their predecessors—had caused it to remain vacant until it is grass-grown, and—one paper has alleged—it has also produced a blackberry bush. It is not often it falls to our lot in this country to name a new town. Of one of the rare occasions when it was thought desirable to rename an old town the capital story is told of how Lord Palmerston suggested that Rugeley should be named after him, as the residents did not relish the fame which had come to the place through its connection with Palmer the poisoner. There are some towns which many people would like to have re-named. A large number of them are in Wales, and about them we need say no more. Oswaldt- wistle, however, though it is the name of an English township, presents difficulties to Englii3ll- - sto try to tsay it (*alp.
