div.p: Everyone is shucked at the THE PROBLEM enormous mortality from OF INDIA. plague among the natives of India, and the most - terrible fact about it is that the superstition of the sufferers is such that they hinder the sanitary and medical measures taken by the Government for their benefit, regarding disease as the act of God. This being the case,such remedial measures as are taken are robbed of much of their effect. In our opinion, two lessons are to be learnt from these facts. In the first place the agitation in favoiar of giving the mass of the natives of India a voice in the Government is,to say the least,prema- ture. On the other han I it appears certain that the existing prejudice of the Anglo-Indian against educating the native must be overcome. It is con- tended, and the statement is irrefutable, that such Indians as have been educated have seldom failed to develop into more or less dangerous opponents of British rule. Eaucatel men deeply resent a con- dition of political servitude. If only the maj -way of Indians were being educated at the same time, so that a reasonable measure of self-government could eventually be extended to them, India would become one of those contented self-governing dominions which are the stable foundation of the British Empire; but while only a minority are educated there is always a danger that they may , stir up their ignorant and fanatical fellow-country- men to deeds of violence. We are not forgetting •the vast extent of our Indian possessions, and the many nationalities living there. The way is long sand difficult. Our contention is that it is the only one which will lead to a satisfactory result, and therefore,however slowly, we ought to be travelling therein.

The Bishop of Birmingham UNIVERSITY served a good cause by his REFORM. advocacy of University reform in the House of 'Lords. True, he did not succeed in getting the Government to promise to appoint a It iyal Corn mission to inqnire into the subject. He was in fact, not particularly anxious for his own success, for he admitted that the time is ng9t really quite ripe for a drastic measure of this kind. But Dr. Gore had an object in bringing forward the topic. It was to apply similar "external stimu- lant" to the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge by which they may be moved to endeavour to realise more fully their places as the centres of the intellectual advancement of England. Dr. Gore has, as an Oxford man, a profound reverence for all the traditions of learning and culture which crowd around the Isis and the Cam. But he considers that the great opportunities which the two ancient Universities possess are not used as they might be for the benefit of the whole of the community. He pointed out effectively how the great students and teachers of the past had in many instances been the sons of humble and poor parents, and emphasised the fact that many of the endowments which support the Colleges at Oxford and Cam- bridge were expressly given for the benefit of such as they. Yet the Universities are crowded with students who have no desire to 2et the full benefit of the culture and instruction. That is what to Dr. Gore, an earnest social reformer working to uplift the people, seems the pity of it. Be sees the materials with which he and those who feel like he does could work being kept in the hands of one class. Perhaps his view is a little exaggerated. Oxford and Cambridge are no longer mediteval. They have been leavened of late years by the abolition of tests and other measures, and by the University Extension movement. But there is much to be done. Probably it would not be best done by a Royal Commission. Oxford and Cambridge must Work out their own salvation in the consciousness that, if they make no advance, they must slowly but surely yield their place as the centres of the intellectual activity of the nation to the newer schools which have sprung up. They cannot live merely upon tradition. It would be unjust to say that nothing has been done. The Bishop of Bristol showed that great advances had been made at Cambridge, and what has been accomplished at Oxfor I, mainly by Oxford men, is for all the world to see. But the progress must not stop there.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

It is reported that Mr. W. C. Anderson, the principal speaker at the Socialist meetings this week, is to be the I.L.P. and Socialist Parliarnentary candi- 'date for Warrington at the next General Election. * * " Sunlight and pure air are God's gifts to all His creatures —wherein have we forfeited our right to them ?" says one of two Warrington housewives who have written to us this week complaining of the smoke nuisance.

• * *. * A new male voice choir is to be heard daily at Latchford. The painters engaged on the periodical -task of renovating the Cantilever Bridge sing vigorously in chorus at their work which, we presume, goes on all the better for the musical strains. * * There is another big libel action in the wind 'Speaking at the Parr's Bank meeting on Thursday Mr. Cecil F. Parr said that the Bank had aniUction pending against a well-known Society paper and had retained Mr. Rufus Isaacs as their counsel. There 'has recently been some very free criticism of various banks in the press and apparently " Parr's " mean to forcibly resent the imputations. * In our "Voice of Labour" column this week, a correspondent signing himself " Socialist Trade Unionist" gives the members of the local trades -unions something to think about. "Warrington trade unionists are" he says, "some of the most reaction- -ary and apathetic of any section of trade unionists in Lancashire and Cheshire." He gives chapter and verse which will not be easily questioned, in support of this sweeping assertion. * * * At Lindfield in Sussex there is an example of what may be termed municipal trading, which seems to act most excellently for the relief of the rates. The parish council is making a business of breeding sWans and they fiad no difficulty in disposing of the cygnets to owners of ornamental waters at 10s. each, thus realising a large profit. Of course, it is not every parish council which has at its disposal a piece of water suited for the purpose, but the example of Lindfield may be of interest to those which have. * * It was rather curious in the soap action to notice how assorted were the polities of the counsel and the parties to the action. Mr. Lever is, of course, a Radical M.P. His counsel included four M.P.'s, two of them, Sir Edward Carson and Mr. F. E. Smith, Unionists, and two, Mr, Horridge and Mr. Hemmerde, Liberals. The defendants, a Unionist newspaper, had for leader Mr. Rufus Issacs, Radical member for Reading, and the duel which decided the fate of the case between Mr. Lever and Mr. Isaacs was, therefore, 'between two fellow Radicals. The defendant's other leading counsel. was Mr. Duke, who, until the last election, was Unionist member for Plymouth.

The worst of all faults is to have none. —RICHARDSON. The origin of hospitality is to appease hostility in a stranger.—NIETZSCIIE. Mr. J. C. Parr indulged in the usual gentle sopil- istries at the Primrose League fete on Saturday. He said they were caught napping at the last general election, but "if he knew the men of Stockton Heath, Latchford, Grappenhall and other places he felt sure they would be more wide awake in future." It is odd -what a difference the point of view makes in a man's Opinions. It snits Mr. Parr to suggest that the electors of the Knutsford Division were not " wide-awake " when they threw over Toryism and class privilege in one great throw. We should have thought that the magnitude of the poll and the directness of intention were evidence of considerable mental activity on the ,part of the electors. Mr. Parr ought to have bade his hearers sleep mice again. They would be more •amenable to his ministration when in a semi-sonseious 1440

Mr. Alan Sykes, the prospecti re Unionist candidate for Knutsford Division, made his bow to the Grappen- hall Primrose Leaguers on Saturday. Rumour has it that the bow was not a great success. Mr. Sykes had very little to say and no political intelligence to impart. His was not a fighting speech and will hardly scare the sitting member, Mr. A. J. King, M.P. In substance all Mr. Sykes said was that " work was the key-note of everything," their motto was "Empire and Liberty " and " they must never lose an oppor- tunity of binding themselves closer to the Colonies." i This s very nice and rosy f3r the Colonies, but as a programme for the agricultural constituency of Knutsford it is not very appetising. " Empire and Liberty " are fine full-sounding phrases but they do not offer much to the elector at home who is con- cerned with work, wages, and social reform.

* * Mr. \V. H. Lever, the plaintiff in the sensational soap case, was (says " London Opinion ") twenty years ag) a grocer in Warrington, and he began soap-making with a capital of £l,OOO. He is a man of medium height, clean-shaven, with a ruddy face and bright, keen eyes. His business success has been phenomenal, and his company has factories not only at Port gunlight just outside Birkenhead, but at Boston, Philadelphia, Toronto and Sydney, as well as in Switzerland, Germany and , Belgium. Lever Brothers, in addition, possess oil mills in America, and the nuts which they buy in Samoa are crushed in Sydney, the oil being sent home and the oil cake sold to Australian farmers. Mr. Lever invented the scheme of prosperity sharing, and his model village at Port Sunlight is one of the best organised communities in the world.

Air. W. C. Anderson, who has this week addresse a series of open-air Labour meetings in Warrington is a typical socialist—typical of the cartoons of the daily press. A vigorous speaker, his strong and mobile features betray the earnestness with which he seeks to convince his hearers. His fervid declamation is accompanied by vigorous gesture, and , wearing a wide-awake on a long and luxuriant crop of black hair, and a light summer suit tin whole picture presented is of a man of unbounded activity filled with the dissatisfaction of a socialist with the present state of society. In his address he is perhaps a trifle superficial and in his endeavours to reach his hearers is apt to be a little pedantic but these are not very serious defects and can be remedied, and in spite of them both he holds his auditors and is listened to with patience. *

Canon Gibson Smith, 1:sTlio was, twenty-sir years ago, a teacher at the Warrington Grammar School, officiated as the principal speaker at the Speech Day on Thursday, and had some interesting things to say about education. It was not religious education, secular education, elementary education, or secondary education that he spoke about, but the education that went to the making of a man. Canon Smith does not set great store by system and the three r's in fitting a youth for the battle of life. "The value and power of education," he said " did not lie in the stores of knowledge which were acquired so much as in the habits a man -acquired, in his intellectual energy, moral power, self-control and resolute subjugation of the body to the mind." Later, in comparing German and English characteristics and educational methods, he quoted Sir Ellis Barker to the effect that "the results of German education were no t superior to those of Great Britain from the point of view of national utility."

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 27, 1907
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 27, 1907

Stockton Heath Garden Society. • The members and friends of the Stockton Heath Garden Society have, during the present week, been in the fortunate position of being able to visit the gardens of the gentry of the district. On Sunday evening, about 30 availed themselves of the privilege accorded them of visiting the charming garden of Mr. William Fletcher, Lower Whitley, and were more than amply repaid for the journey thither. On Tuesday even- ing the ever-popular visit was paid to Sir G.Greenall's, Walton Hall. Large numbers found great pleasure in a stroll round these lovely grounds, which have never looked better or been in more perfect order. The roses especially met with very great admiration. On Thursday the picturesque gardens of the President of the Society, Mr. V. B. Davies, attracted a goodly con- course. These gardens are always a source of delight and on this occasion, as previously, were admired as they so richly deserve. A busy week, a member writes, but one of undoubted pleasnre to all who made it convenient to be present. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SFIOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adtv. CHINA. TEA SETS.—Special show of latest art 1 patterns. See windows, J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge- street, Warrington.—Advt. ; Water Polo Match. There was a large attendance at the Warrington IBaths on Thursday evening when the return water polo match in the Liverpool and District League was played between Warrington and St. Helens. Quite 11500 people were present and a keenly contested ! match was witnessed. In fact the excitement at one " stage was responsible for two members of the crowd giving an unrehearsed item by falling into the shallow end of the bath. At the commencement of the game I St. Helens had the disadvantage of defending the deep 'end of the baths, but they at once attacked and Lomax • put on the first goal. Pressure was maintained, but Warrington rallied and after a hot attack Allen equalised with a grand shot. No further scoring took • place up to the interval. On resuming, Warrington had the best of matters, but St. Helens forced them back and Sharrocks gave the visitors the lead. War- rington played up pluckily, and C. Ashton again equalised matters. After this, however, St. Helens showed superior form, and goals were scored in quick succession by Sharrocks, Burrows, and Ripley. Final : St. Helens, 5 goals; Warrington, 2 goals. The second round of the Works Squadron Competition was swam off during the evening, the Co-operative Stores beating Peter Walker and Sons. and Pearson and Knowles beating the Post Office. PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. NEW STRAWBERRY JAM.—ASHLEY'S Sankey st.— Advt.

----- Drowned in a Works Reservoir. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington yesterday on the body of John Stamp, four years of age, son of Arthur Stamp, Orford-street, who was drowned in the reservoir at OockhedgeMills.lt appeared from the evidence that,deceased and another lad named Stanley Pickering minaged to get through a small hole at the bottom /of the wall surrounding the reservoir, which had been made for the purpose of carrying out certain work. They got on the , edge of i the reservoir, and the deceased, n trying to reach a stick, fell in and was drowned. The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death. •

I WHITE CITY, MANCHESTER.

Summer has fairly set in, let us hope that it has come to stay. From the time of the opening of the White City at Old Trafford, Manchester, which by the way is the only Amusement Park in Great Britain, until a short time ago, the weather has either been too cold or disagreeable for the masses to patronise outdoor amuse- ment. Yet it is a fact that this City of pleasure has been doing a large business despite the inclemeut weather, and has been a surprise, as well as surpassing all expectations of the Management. They are offering amusement attractions and entertainment,which I compare favourably with the best parks in America I and Europe, while it possesses natural advantages which are not surpassed anywhere. Their motto is "Nothing is too good for our public." The Free Circus is now one of the established features. The bills are varied and are changed frequently. One of the newest free attractions shortly to be presented will be called , "The Venetian Fete," in which Gondolas, Native I Gondoliers and Singers, will form a principal feature. New Side Shows are being added and varied. Hales Tours of the World is without question the most interesting achievement of mechanical invention— this novelty is the first realisation of a lon.' sought want" It is wonderful" says Charles Reid, "how genius can borrow," and Oliver Wendell Holmes remarks that "A good image is like a diamond which may be set a hundred times in as many generations, and gain new beauty with each change." Just so with Hales Tours of the World—it is a diamond to those who have made one of its tours, for with each succeeding change one finds new beauty—and those who have not as yet enjoyed this delightful educational and instructive amusement, have surely something in store for them. The uninitiated tourists will never know the real fascina- tion that these tours exert until they have tried them. In fact it is the most realistic production ever attempted. I Cars are now being run successfully in London, White I City Manchester Blackpool, llublia, Glasgow, Leeds, I etc., and other places will be added as soon as cars can I be completed.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A MUSICAL NUISANCE.

Eleven men, residing in the neighbourhood of Chancery-lane and Fleet-lane, were charged at St. Helens on Monday with breach of the peace. The evi- dence showed that on Saturday, the 13th inst., one of Parr brass bands had been away at Manchester and won a prize in a contest. It was very late when the band got back, and a large number of men waited at Parr Stocks. Police-constable O'Donnell came on the scene at a quarter to o'clock on Sunday morning and began to disperse them. He told the magistrates that the men caused a great disturbance and that this was the practice every week-end. The men went about play- ing concertinas, 8:,c., and disturbed the neighbourhood so that the people could not get any sleep. Hill and Dolan were discharged and the other nine were bound over to keep the peace. ORANGEMEN'S PARADE.

There was an unusually large muster at the St. Helens Orangemen's annual parade at St. Peter's Church, Parr, on Sunday. The St. Helens lodges of the Order were reinforced by a good number of members from Liver- pool, Bootle, Ashton, Haydock and Earlestown. Over 500 members were present altogether, in addition to the Colonel Sanderson band and the Protestant Boys' band, Liverpool. Prov. Grand Master John Holding, of Liverpool; Prov. Grand Treasurer Stewart M'Coy ; District Master Watson, of Buckley; District Master Phillips, Liverpool; and District Mester Lester,Bootle; were present, as wall as District Master P. Dickinson; D.D.M. John Bradbury, District Treasurer James Robinson, and District Seuetary Thomas Isherwood. The Rev. W. Edmondson, vicar of Parr, preached. He said the chief thing tue,7 ought to strive after was Christian consistency. If Ile leaders in Church and State were more consistent there would be far less , anarchy, and far less Romaaaising in their dear old
IReformed Church of England; there would be far less criticism of Orangemen and of the Church Association, I and there would be far less need for either of them. 1 HOTOR CLUB FOR ST. HELENS.

A St. Helens and District Motor Club has been formed with a membership of close on forty. Councillor A. Rudd presided at the meeting, and was elected cap- tain, with Mr. Ralph Milne vice-captain, and Mr. T. Gregory hon. secretary and treasurer.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON,
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON,
STREET BETTING.

On Thursday, at Newton, John Smith, of Haydock, was fined £5 and costs for street betting in Back Blackbrook-road on the 24th irst. Two police-constables watched Smith receive slips and money and arrested him.

div.head: OPEN-AIR SERVICE.
div.p: OPEN-AIR SERVICE.

An open-air service was held an Sunday evening on the recreation ground belonging to the Y.11.C.A. The Rev. Simon C. Hall,of the Earlestown Wesleyan Cnurch, conducted. Special anthems weae rendered by members of the choir.

ACCIDENT AT THE WAGGON WORKS. On Saturday, while engaged in breaking up old wheels in the London and North-Western Railway Company's Waggon Works, a man named James Wainwright had his foot badly injured through a piece of the metal striking him. He was conveyed home and medically attended, and is progressing favourably.

div.head: YOUNG MEN'S CATEIOLIC ASSOCIATION.
div.p: YOUNG MEN'S CATEIOLIC ASSOCIATION.

The formal opening of the club of the Young Men's Catholic Association in Fairc/ough-street, took place on Sunday evening, the Rev. Father O'Reilly presiding. The house in Fairclough-street lately occudied by the Y.M.C.A. has been taken over for the purpose, and curiously enough the initials are still available. CONSERVATIVE WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION. The Newton and Earlestown Conservative Working lien's Association had a very successful picnic on Saturday. Leaving Earlestown by the 1.14 p.m. ordinary train for Chester, where they visited at their leisure the places of interest. The party of 70 afterwards met at the Cestria Cafe for tea. The rest of the evening was spent in sight-sesing and rambling round the walls. &c., and all assembled at the station in time for the 8.50 p.m. train, Earlestown being reached shortly after ten o'clock. SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHELSY PICNIC.

The St. John's Sunday school teachers held their annual picnic on Saturday. As in former years a com- mittee was formed to select the place and to make all arrangements. It consisted of Messrs. Greening, Hardman and Cave, and Misses Dollin, Singleton, Bailey and Watkinson, who chose Chester. Leaving Earlestown by the 8.45 a.m. train the visitors reached the city shortly before tee. The Cathedral, walls, and town were the chief attractions in the morning and the party met at Cottle's Cafe for dinner, and afterward" boating on the Dee was largely enjoyed.

SEQUEL TO A COLLIERY STRIKE. lug At Newton Petty Sessions on Thursday John and James Morgan, of Golborne, were summoned by Edward Donnelly for assault on the 13th inst. The case for the presecution stated by Mr. J. W. Knowles was that there was a strike on at the Old Bryn Colliery, Ashton-in- Makerfield, and that complainant's step-son, who was employed at the colliery, was in the habit of working over-time. Defendants met complainant, and told him that that must be stopped; but when they received the reply that he had nothing to do with his step-son's work one knocked him down and the other kicked him. The defence, as stated by Mr. E. White, was that Donnelly used foul language. John Morgan was fined 10s. and costs, but the ease against the brother was dismissed.

div.head: DROWNING CASE SEQUEL..
div.p: DROWNING CASE SEQUEL..

William Thomaa,collier, of Cherry-street, Earlestown, made a third appearance since Friday last at St. Helens Police Court on Tuesday in connection with the adven- tures of himself and a man named John Mitchell, of Earlestown, who was drowned on Thursday night in a a reservoir at Ashton's Green Colliety. The evidence was that the two men walked from Earlestown to St. Helens on Thursday night for some money. Later Thomas was arrested when taking ewe of Mitchell's clothing by the side of the reservoir, where Mitchell's body was afterwards found. He was brought before the magistrates on Friday, but the cese was adjourned, and Thomas next appeared in Court to give evidence at the inquest on Nionday evening. The magistrates on Tuesday after hearing the evislence, decided to dismiss the case

div.head: FATAL MIDNIGHT SWIM..
div.p: FATAL MIDNIGHT SWIM..

At St. Helens Town Hall on Monday Mr. Brighouse inquired into the extraordinary circumstances connected with the death of John Mitchell, aged thirty-three, collier, of 82, Athol-street, Earlestown, whose body was recovered from the reservoir, near Ashton's Green Colliery, early on Saturday morning. The evidence was that Mitchell walked from Earlestown on Thursday night last to the R taw Inn, Worsley Brow, Sutton, with a man named William Thomas, collier, of Cherry- I street, Earlestown, to draw some money from the Collins I Green branch of the Miners' Federation. On the way back home Mitchell undressed and went for a swim, and was never seen alive afterwards.—Martin Mitchell, brother, gave evidence of identification, and said that on a previous occasion, about two years ago, when under the influence of drink, Mitchell took off his clothes and jumped into the canal.—William Thoiros said they had 12s. to draw from the federation. They landed at'the Railway Inn about twenty minutes past six, and left at ten minutes to eleven at night. They ' had no drink h,nfore they got there, because they had no money. Afterwards they had four pints of beer each. Witness was not drunk, but the deceased was somewhat under the iPfilletlCO of drink. On the way back Mitchell persisted in going for a swim, although he tried to persuade him not to. Witness waited for about three-quarters of an hour by the side of decrast i's clothing, and then began to shout for help. Police- constable Trail came on the scene, and Thomas was locked up.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, who appeared for the landlord of the Railway Inn, Thomas said there would be nearly 200 men at the meeting, and the house was very busy. His friend was quiet, and would not attract the attention of the landlord ,in any way by his conduct.—Robert Lyon, of 126, Berry's-lane, Sutton, spoke to seeing Mitchell in the water about four o'clock on Saturday morning and getting him out.—Police- constable Trail described finding Thomas sitting by the clothing and locking him up. In answer to the coroner, witness admitted that Thomas told him a clear and straightforward tale, something like what he had told here.—A verdict of " Accidentally crowned" was eturned.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

The services in connection with the dedication and opening of the new organ were continued on Sunday, when the preacher was the Rev. Joseph Manning. Special hymns were sung by the children, and solos were given by Miss Mabel Henshall and Mr. E. Robinson Roberts. The choir ably sang the anthems " Send out Thy Light " (Gounod) in the morning, and "Hallelujah Chorus " in the evening. After the evening service, Mr. Frank Hickman gave an admirable recital on the organ, the programme being as follows :—Grand Offer- toire in C Minor, Batiste ; (a) Cantilene, Higgs ; (b) Barcarolle, Wolstenholme ; Prelude and Fugue, from Sonata 6, Rheinberger ; Overtere, Suppe ; choruses were also rendered by the Warrington Male Voice Prize Choir.

Warrington's New Melhodist Minister. The members of the Legh-street Primitive Methodist. Church on Sunday accorded a hearty welcome to their new pastor, the Rev. J. B. Buglass. There was a good congregation at Legh-street in the morning when Mr. Buglass preached his inaugural address. Basing his remarks on the text " For Christ is all and in all," he said he believed that Christ took a real and vital interest in their lives. They had been hearing a great deal about the "new theology," but latterly it had fallen flat. Why was that ? It was because Christ had been taken out of it. Personally he thanked Mr. Campbell—although he by no means agreed with him—for the interest he had aroused in the hearts of the people regarding the higher life. He (the speaker) had seen a few years of life,and he felt that he had no need to change his position or his views regarding Christ. He recognized Him as the all in all in his life. . .

_ Mr. Bugloss again addressed a large congregation in the evening. At this service the choir ably rendered the anthem "Abide with me," under the conductorship of Mr. Spruce. Mr. P. Clatworthy presided at the organ. A camp meeting was held at Latchford during the day at which addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. B Buglass, Messrs. Billingtor, Atkin, Faulkner and Whitley. A formal and hearty welcome was extended to the Rev. J. B. and Mrs. Bugloss on Thursday evening. A well-attended t3a was het' followed by a public meet- ing over which Mr. R. Bridge presided. In welcoming the new pastor, Mr. Whitley assured Mr. Bugloss of the unanimous support which th 3 members of the Warrington Circuit would accord to him. He appealed to the members of the denomination to lend their hearty co-operation to their new pastor. No matter how gifted a man was he could not do much good work unless he had the support of his people, and therefore he asked them all to stand by Mr. Bugloss and to assist him in forwarding the interest of the Warrington circuit. Mr. J. R. Griffiths se:..onded the resolution of welcome which Mr. Whitley moved in concluding, and in doing so advocated the adoption of the practice of mot., systematic giving. Mr. J. BISSELL, on behalf of the Sunday school, sup- ported the motion, as did also Mr. 3. Cotterill on behalf of Latchford Primitive Methodists. In reply Mr. Buglass said he hoped they would all endeavour to keep up the attendance at Church on Sunday. He also supported systematic giving. During the evening solos ‘vere rendered by Miss Bridge and Mr. Curran.

div.head: VOICE OF LABOUR.
div.p: THE VOICE OF LABOUR.
Edited by John Workman.

Readers of this column are invited to assist irs making it interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to make their letters and notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the column. M.S.S. must be addressed to John Workman, " Examiner " Office, Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.

div.head: OBJECT LESSONS
div.p: OBJECT LESSONS

The results of the Jarrow and Comae Valley Bye- Elections are splendid examples of what can be done by the united action of the Trade Unionists and Socialists. Whilst we in Warrington have been wasting our time discussing the question of "Unity" and creating dis-union, the men and women in other constituencies have been organizing their forces, and carrying on a systematic, and alcaost continuous educational propaganda. In Warrington, the educa- tion of the workers in Labour politics has been left almost entirely to the Independent Labour Party, and judging from the large and enthusiastic audiences which have listened to Mr. Anderson at Bridge Foot during the week, there is a strong and growing Socialist opinion in the Borough. Warrington is frequently referred to, by labour leaders visiting the town, as an ideal conttituency, both from an industrial and geographical paint of view. It is of comparatively small area fora Parlia- mentary constituency, with not less than Ta per cent. of the electors belonging to what is called the working classes.

It is when we turn to the tradesman section of the electorate that we find the- least hopefal signs of • progress in labour politics. As one who knows some- thing of both the National and local Labour movement, I don't hesitate to say that Warrington trades unionists, as a body, are some of the most reactionary and apathetic •of any section of trades unionists in Lanca- shire and Cheshire.

llnstead of receiving the co-operation and assistance of the higher paid trades unionists, the local Labour organisations have been met with opposition at every point. In the Warrington Labour Representation Com- mittee there was an organisation to which the trade unionists ought to have given their loyal and• enthusiastic support, instead of which they allowed it to" starve" and to practically waste away, until it became a burden on those who have bravely tried to again restore it to health and vigour. Instead of unity of the labour forces, the trade, unionists are' divided into Liberals, Tories and Labourites, with a small and insignificant section who are attached to those organisaticus called the Pro- gressive Labour League and Conservative Labour Party. Objections have been raised to the local L.R.C. and the I.L.P. on the most flimsy pretexts by those trade unionists Who are opposed to Latour politics. The question of paying one penny or twopence extra con- tributions per year is sufficient fcr some of them to hang objections upon, whilst all the time they are forgetting the broad principles which should weld the Labour forces together. The workers have for so long been accustomed to having thei: politics paid for by landlords and employers of labour who having "paid the piper have called the tune," that it appears to be difficult for many of them to learn that if Labour is to be represented as,a should be, the worlears must be pre- pared to pay for their own politics ungrudgingly and I adequately. I don't hesitate to say that every shilling paid by the workers foe Labour Representation will bring to them a better return that twenty shillings paid for purely trades union purposes on the old lines. Why then object any longer to cooperate with the Socialists? It is the work of the I.L.P. that made a Labour Party possible. It is the members of the I.L.P. who bring into all elections that enthusiasm and energy which has brought success to the Labour candidates in the various constitutencies. There is not a single member of the Labour Party in the House of Commens who will not declare that the I.L.P. section of his supporters were the, best workers. The Warrington trade unionists therefore have. nothing to loose by co-operation with the I.L.P.,rather have thy a go id deal to gain. If we are to have 1" Unity " let us have it in reality, and so weld I together the labour forces that we can follow the ex- ample set by Jarrow, Colne -Valley and other con-. stituencies. This is the aim of one who can sign him- self a
SOCIALIST TRADE UNIONIST:.

div.head: "POLITICAL BIGOTS."
div.p: "POLITICAL BIGOTS."
Mr. H. Vivian, M.P., Resents Trade
Union Censure.
HIS ACTION AT JARROW.

The General Council of the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners of Manchester having passed a, vote of censure on Mr. Henry Vivian, M.P., for supporting the Liberal candidate in the Jarrow by- election, Arr. Vivian has replied as follows to the general secretary of the Society. Dear Mr. Chandler,— . . 1 suggust tha's it is con- trary to the spirit and constitution of the union for a member's action to be discussed and judgment given without his having an opportunity to put his view of the case. . . . I regret that the administration of the affairs of our union has passed into the hands of men whose political partisanship, judged by this reso- lution, prevents them from seeing that such action on their part is a misuse of their power as officials of a trade Onion. They have no more right as officials of the union to dictate to me, or any other member of the union, what political opiuions I should hold or express than they have to say what church I should attend. It is the right and duty of every citizen to form his own opinions freely on matters of this sort, and any pressure which tends to prevent this is tyrannical, whether it is put on by a political league, an employer of labour, or the Council of a trada union. Your Council's motives are, no doubt, good, as were those of the prime movers in the Inquisition which tortured people's bodies in order to save their souls. They were religious bigots. Your Council appears to be made up of political bigots intent upon saving myself and other members of our union from political error, I not by the only righteous course open to them—viz., by propagating in their capacity as citizens political truth—but by resolutions which may have the effect of frightening timid members of the union into the belief that unless they act politically in the way prescribed by the General Council of the Union they may be fined, expelled, lose benefits for which they have paid for years, or in other ways suffer. A trade union or any other organization has no right to attract people into it, take their money for years under a profession of one set of objects, and then permit its officials to use the influence of the union. for promoting other objects ; and, above all, it has no right to hold members up to odium in the organization because they refuse to abandon the political views they believe in. The problems of life are so complex that no one organization of human beings can claim to repres nit the whole truth, and unless separate associa- tions for dealing with separate problems are perinitted there can be no true freedom.

I feel sure the Council do not realise the injury this policy will do to our union if it is present all along the line. I have evidence from all parts of the country that our members resent it, and of course those who do so must be credited with the same determination, courage, and honesty as the General Council. I shall always be willing to meet the Council and defend my action, and hope it will see its way to withhold its hand from allowing political partisanship to split the trade union ranks and cause great injury to the members. lam sending a copy of Mill's essay on " Liberty " for each member of the Council in the hope that the spirit it breathes may have some influence on the minds of the members of the Council. . .—Yours, etc., HENRY V EVIAN.

div.head: BEYOND FATHER'S CONTROL.
div.p: BEYOND FATHER'S CONTROL.

At Widnes, on Thursday morning, a young girl named Elizabeth Walton, residing at Mill-lane, Middlewick, pleaded guilty to a charge of stealing a silver watch, value 305., and a pair of boots, value lOs the property of A. Matthews, Catherine-street, and also to a charge of stealing a lady's jacket, value 10s., the property of Mrs. Hughes, James-street. Het habit was to visit houses late at night, tell a lamentable story of having nowhere to go, and she was taken in. On both occasions she was left in the house whilst the women went out to make purchases, and upon their return articles were found missing and the woman gone.—Detective- sergeant Davidson said her father was a respectable man, but latterly she had got begond his management. There was a record against her for this class of 9flence. She was sent to gaol for one month. Addressing the silver dealer, the Chairman said they considered that he had acted in a very injudicious manner in this case, and to mark. their displeasure they would disallow costs.

div.head: FIRTH COMPANY's PICNIC.
div.p: FIRTH COMPANY's PICNIC.

A good number of the Firth Company Employees joarneyea to the Axe and Cleaver, Bollington on Satur- day and, says a member, "the weather was delightful and nature met our gaze with a bounteous display of her best raiment the drive along the country • lanes affording us as town dwellers much pleasure. In spite of the rumbling vehicle the birds could be heard twittering in the hedge rows and the skylarks trilling overhead. On each side of the road were fields of golden-corn waving in the gentle breeze and the scent of new mown hay mingled with the fragrance from the cottage gardens wafted beneath our nostrils. Occasion- ally we drove through shaded lanes lined with stately oaks and majestic elms, tly3 tall poplars and towering beech trees being conspicuous among them. The rendezvous was reached in good time, coats were dis- carded and the battle of bowls began, the green proving a hard task master owing owing to its uneven surface and excitement, pleasure and annoyance were much in evidence on the faces of the players. There was much speculation whether the novices or the practiced bowlers were the best. After two rounds the party adjourned for tea. A spacious apartment was provided and the vegetarian or beef eater was able to satisfy the inner -man and judging from the bustle of the waiters during the attack and the appearance of the tables afterwards I think everybody did justice to his appetite. Tea over Mr. A. Rathbone occupied the chair a round of applause greeting him.He said it was usual to propose a vote of thanks but be was not going to make a speech and he would call upon Mr. Reeves to propose a vote of thanks to the Secretary. Mr. Reeves on rising said he had much pleasure in proposing a vote Pf thanks to Mr. Frank Rathbone who had so kindly and successfully carried out the arrange- ments for the day. He (Mr. Reeves) knew it bad involved a lot of work and time to make the picnic a success and be would only be expressing the feeling of all present when he said the best thanks of the gather- ing were due to Mr. F. Rathbone for the able manner in which he had carried out the arrangements. Personally be had enjoyed himself and hoped it would not be the last picnic of its kind as it brought about a better social feeling one with another. He would also like to add to the vote of thanks an appreciation of the presence of the managing directors of the firm Mr. A. Ratbbone and Mr.S. Taylor,also the managers Mr. J. Sims and Mr. D. Birrell. In these days of combines and trusts work- men hardly ever saw their employers and when they did see them did not know them. He was pleased to say that was not the case at Florence Mills.

Mr. J. Sims seconded. Mr. F. Rathbone responded saying it had given him great pleasure to get the picnic up and the best thanks that could be given to him was to see everybody enjoying themselves. A vote of thanks was then given to the Host and Hostess and responded to. The bowling NMS then resumed ending after much ,excitement with a win for J. Daintith and H. Emmerson. The return journey was then commenced in the gentle and cooling breeze all arriving home with pleasant recollections."

div.p: ADVICE WORTH TAKING.

A very general complaint, especially among people 'of middle age, is rheumatism. So numerous are the people who suffer from it that most of the advertised patent specifics refer to it as one of the diseases which they cure. Frequently rteumatism will yield to treat- ment, but it is not reaqonable to expert that the rheumatic acid can be eliminated from the system by -any external application of liniment. Temporary relief is afforded by rubbing, but the cure must be something which will prevent a further making of the rheumatic acid and its distribution into the various muscles and joints of the body. Care should be taken 'in the diet, and meat and alcoholic liquors be very sparingly taken. div.head: Labour Bureau.
div.p: Labour Bureau.

During the week there have been registered 53 persons, making 875 registered during the current year. Twenty-two situations have been offered by employers during the week, and there are now on the register out of employment 189 persons. The follow- ing is a list of the different trades :—General labourers, 34 ; builders' labourers, 4 ; wire trade labourers, 10 ; ironworks' labourers, 25 ; tanners' labourers, 4 ; joiner, 1 ; engine drivers and firemen, 12 ; fitters, 3 ; carters, 8 ; sundry other trades, 17; -youths, 15 ; girls, 7 ; women for charring and daily ,cleaning, 44; sundry other women, 5. During the Week several ladies have made use of the Bureau for Women for charring and daily work, and it is to he hoped that every lady will soon realize the utility of the Bureau when requiring women and girls for household work of any description, and that the female department in the near future may become a very useful agency to the ladies and to those who seek -employment.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 27, 1907. SCIENCE NOTES AND NEW
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 27, 1907. SCIENCE NOTES AND NEW
TIDES AND THE EARTH'S CRUST. I

The theory that the earth's crust is sub- jet to daily movements analogous to tides ' has been confirmed by the seismograph (in- strument to measure earthquakes) at Mauri- tius. The movements seem to depend upon , the sun. A wave of low barometric pressure ' travels round the earth after the sun, and this wave causes a bulge in the crust beneath it. ;

div.head: LARGE CASTING.
div.p: A LARGE CASTING.

One of the largest iron castings ever turned out of a foundry was poured in the foundry of the Mestra Machine Company, Pittsburg, and weighs 201,0001 b. when finished, the requisite 220,0001 b. of metal being obtained from six furnaces. The cast- ing forms the bed plate on the low pressure side of a cross compound c.ondensing piston engine to be used for driving the finishing rolls of the new rail mill of the Bethlehem Steel Company.

div.head: 5,000 FACETS IN BEETLE'S EYES.
div.p: 5,000 FACETS IN BEETLE'S EYES.

A little-known phase of entomology is dis- cussed by Herr Leinemann on the number of facets in the eyes of insects. He has had the patience to count the facets in the eyes of 150 species of beetles, and finds that the larger the specimen the more numerous are the facets, and that usually there is not much difference in the sexes. The male in many cases, however, has more facets than the female. Some beetles have as many as 5,000 facets. There is no general reduction in noc- turnal species.

div.head: IMPORTANCE OF INDIAN LORE.
div.p: IMPORTANCE OF INDIAN LORE.

The American Ethnological Society has be- gun a series of publications of authentic material collected among native American tribes. It is pointed out that hitherto little has been collected in their own language concerning the customs, beliefs, and ideas of the natives. Yet authentic records of infor- mation given by the Indians are regarded as of prime importance for a thorough study 'of the ethnology and early history of the Ameri- caa continent. The Indians are believed to possess much valuable knowledge not yet recorded.
THE LIMIT OF HUMAN STRENGTH.

Experiments upon a number of men hare shewn that a man sft. high and weighing 1261 b. will lift on an average 1561 b. through a vertical distance of Bin., or 2171 b. through a height of I•2in. Others 6.lft. high and weigh- ing 1831 b. could lift the 1561 b. to a height of 13in., or 2171 b. to a height of 6in. Other me; 6ft. 3in. high and weighing 1881 b. could lift 1561 b. to a height of 16m., or 2171 b. to a height of 9in. By a variety of experiments it was shewn that the average human strength is equivalent to raising 301 b. through a dis- tance of 2-ift. in one second.

div.head: HORSE'S ANCESTORS.
div.p: THE HORSE'S ANCESTORS.

Lovers of horses may be delighted with the distinguished genealogy which geologists have finally completed for that favoured animal—at least, the names of the horse's ancestors look very distinguished. Here is the list, with the geological eras in which each lived, as arranged by an American scientist, Mr. W. IT. Rice: The line of de- scent begins with Hyracotherium and Eohip- pus of the lower Eocene Age. Then follow Protorohippus and Orohippus of the middle Eocene; Epihippus of the upper Eocene; Mesohippus of the Oligocene; Anchitherium of the lower Miocene; Parahippus, Proto- hippus, and •Pliohippus of the middle and upper Miocene; and finally Equus of the Pliocene and the Quaternary, from which the modern horse directly descends. Hip- parion and Hippidium represented ancient side branches that died without descendants.

div.head: UNSOUND CEREALS AND INSANITY.
div.p: UNSOUND CEREALS AND INSANITY.

A French doctor has reported to the Academy of Medicine a distinctive phase of insanity which, as to its causes, is novel to European science' though, unhappily, far from new in itself. Dr. A. Marie, a practi- tioner in mental cases in Paris was staying in Egypt, and. in visiting an asylum at Alex- andria found himself so much attracted by a for.:A of insanity which seemed to be almost peculiar to the Arabs that he entered upon its study. Starting from the observation that nearly all the victims of this form of mania were also afflicted with the pellagra or skin disease of the country, he finally evolved the conclusion that it results from the habitual consumption of cereals in an unsound state. From this one is tempted to speculate upon it further. Pellagra is common enough in Italy, and the question arises as to whether it produces a similar form of insanity.

div.head: ANIMALS AS DISEASE – CARRIERS.
div.p: ANIMALS AS DISEASE - CARRIERS.

The eat has long been under suspicion, and has been accused of disseminating diph- theria; among other diseases; but Dr. Rem- linger has made some bacteriological experi- ments on the retention, of infective organisms in the fur of dogs and cats which, the British, Medical Journal considers, give greater precision to the charge. In experi- ments upon cats it was found that the typhoid bacillus persisted in the hair up to the seventeenth day; on the twentieth day it had disappeared. The diphtheria bacillus persisted until the twenty-fourth day, but had disappeared on the twenty-seventh. A twenty-four hours' culture of the bacillus, isolated on the twenty-fourth day, was inocu- lated subcutaneously in a dose of 1 c.cm. into a guinea-pig weighing 470 grams, and killed the animal in thirty hours. There was, there- fore, no attenuation ,of virulence. Other disease germs proved more or less persistent. Experiments on dogs gave results very much the same as those obtained with cats.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC nußits.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC nußits.

A further development has taken place re- cently concerning the so-called " scientific " ruby 'question, says a writer in the Watch- maker and Jeweler. These imitations are being produaed in large sizes and of the colour of fine pink topazes, to which they be‘r a very good resemblance, and are there- foze called scientific pink topazes. This is quite a misnomer, however, as they answer to the usual tests of hardness, specific gravity, and refractive index. If the Herbert Smith refractometer is used for the latter, they can be distinguished immediately, as the shadow line being beyond the range of the instru- ment is not given, while that of topaz is very distinct. It will also be found on examina- tion with a magnifying - glass that these pro- ductions contain many glassy - looking bub- bles, and the " dust " (which is really a mass of minute bubbles) can sometimes be seen to lie in curved layers, the curves being caused by the bead or cone-like formation of the original "brut." The hardness, specific gravity, and refractive index are the same as those belonging to the genuine ruby. The hardness of the topaz, being considerably less, is, therefore, easily scratched by these specimens.

div.head: CAVE DWELLERS IN SAHARA.
div.p: CAVE DWELLERS IN SAHARA.

A discovery of curious interest has been made by Mr. Hans Vischer, the English resi- dent at Kuka on Lake Chad, in Northern i Nigeria, Africa, n the course of exploration in the Sahara desert. In the country around the Gharian mountains a colony of cave dwellers was found. The strange inhabitants of 'these subterranean residences excavate a huge, deep hole in the ground, which forms a kind of quadrangle or courtyard, reached by means of narrow entrances about 30ft. in length by 3ft. broad. All the rooms and other apartments of the occupiers open upon this courtyard, and are

EXCAVATED OUT OF THE SOLID EARTH upon all sides, the internal lighting of the apartments being s gained from the aperture opening upon the quadrangle. The rooms themselves are very dark. To protect the dwellings underneath, there is a wall which is carried right round the courtyard. A re- markable feature of this strange community is the absolute cleanliness that prevails everywhere. In strange contrast to these sub- terranean villages are the remains to be ob- served on all sides of Roman dwellings, and evidences of their occupation scattered in- congruously among the primitive habitations of the natives.

I expect many of you are making your preparations for the usual summer holiday. Well, wherever you go, I hope you will have a downright good time. Perhaps, after all the rain that we have had you may be fortunate in getting some nice bright weather. None of us can enjoy ourselves quite so much if the weather is dull and rainy.

Although you may be away from home, do not forget that I shall be expecting to receive many pretty post cards during July and August as mentioned in my letter last week. I am sure you will like the lovely boxes of Fry's chocolate that I shall give to the six members sending the best cards to me. With love to all, yours affec- tionately, UNCLE NED.

div.p: WELCOME TO Lena Cann, Lizzie Holt, Arthur Spencer, Reginald Spencer.
THE BOYS AND THE APPLES.

Two boys, Dick and Tom, went out for a walk. At the end of a long, green lane they came to an orchard, in whioh grew some apple trees. They thought the apples must be nice, for they looked quite ripe. "I should like some apples off that tree." "So should I," said Dick. "Shall we get some?" said Tom. "They are not ours." They will be when we have got them," said Tom, With a laugh. "No," said Dick, "for, though we get them, we must Arst steal them from the man whose orchard this is, so they cannot be ours." "Well, no one will see us," said Tom, "and if you fear to come with me, I will climb over the hedge and get them myself. You can stand there, and if the man happens to come round, you whistle, and I will run back." "1 could not do that, Tom," said Dick. "You are a goose." "You can do as you choose. I shall go and get some apples." So Tom climbed over the hedge, and thought he was quite safe, but the owner was behind the hedge, and had heard all that the boys had said. He had a big stick in his hand, and as soon as Tom got dowi4, to the ground, he caught Vold of him by the collar, and gave him a good thrashing. "There," said the man, "take that. I will teach you how to lay your hands on what is not your own." The man said to Dick: "Come with me and get as many apples as you like, for you are a good boy." Dick went and got a lot of apples, and his mother was very pleased with him for not stealing. LIZZIE HOLT.

div.head: TERRIFIED HIS WIFE.
div.p: TERRIFIED HIS WIFE.

Bill Jones is a country storekeeper down in Louisiana, and last spring he went to New Orleans to purchase a stock of goods. The goods were shipped at once, and reached home before he did. When the goods were delivered at his store by the carrier, Bill's wife hap- pened to be there. She looked at the largest package. She uttered a loud cry, and called for a hammer. A neighbour rushed to her assi9tance, and asked what was the matter. The wife, pale and trembling, pointed to the inscrip- tion on the box, which read as follows: "Bill inside." LENA CANN.

div.head: PLENTY OF TIME.
div.p: PLENTY OF TIME.

"By Jove, ii-Te7;--6ei-m-y-trainl" were the words that caught the ears of many people standing on a London and North-Western sta- tion platform in the Midlands a few days ago; and a short, fat man, with a top hat, hurried through the gates like a thunderbolt and ran down the platform with the speed of, a rolling hat in a gale of wind. He held his bag in one hand, and sprinted as though it were a matter of life and death. The train shot out towards the end of the plat- form, but still the short man continued the race, puffing and blowing as he went, to the amuse- ment of the many spectatdrs who were watch- ing him. The little fellow was game, and finally, after a herculean effort, reached the train, threw his bag into an open compartment, and clambered in. Then he sank down and lay as limp as a rag 'after his 'Prodigious exertions. The next moment the train backed into the station once more. The other passengers got in at their leisure; and it was not less than ten minutes before the train started off again. Meanwhile the little fat man was hiding him- self behind a. newspaper.

"AFTER YOt 1" A well-known barrister relates the following story with great gusto. Some time ago he had under cross-examination a youth from the country who rejoiced in the name of Samson, and whose replies were provocative of much laughter in the court. "And so," questioned the barrister, "you wish the court to believe that you are a peace- fully disposed and inoffensive kind of person?"

"And that you have no desire to follow in the steps of your illustrious namesake, and smite the Philistines I" "No, I've not," answered the witness. "And if I had the desire I ain't got the power at present." "Then you think you would be unable to cope successfully with a thousand enemies, and utterly rout them with the jawbone of an ass?" "Well," answered the ruffled Samson, "I might have a try when you have done with the weapon!"

div.head: "WHAT THE CZAR READS.
div.p: "WHAT THE CZAR READS.

It is useless ior- a Russian editor to put any jokes in his paper, hoping to tickle the Czar, for his high protected majesty never reads them. He doesn't read anything in the papers except such carefully sifted matter as an ex- perienced censor prepares for the royal eye. It is the duty of this censor to get up very early in the morning—earlier than the earliest news- boy, in fact—so that he may read advance sheets of the various journals, damp from the press, and select such matter as. may be best calculated to gratify the Czar and stimulate his appetite for breakfast. Nothing about bombs or dynamite must be allowed to creep in, or the cendor would lose, his situation. These siftings are then copied on sheets of fine paper, and after another in- spection by a higher dignitary, they are de- posited on his Majesty's table ready for his perusal. Any person whose indignation has been: aroused by reading accounts of Siberian cruel- ties, and and who contemplates writing "An Open. Letter to the Car" for a St. Petersburg journal, might as well relinquish the idea. The Czar would never see it, even if it were pub- lished.
"Always pay as you go," said an old man to. his nephew. "But, uncle, suppose I have nothing to pay- With?" "Then don't go."

div.head: THEY WENT:
div.p: THEY WENT:

A well-known professor at one of our Univer- sities was often annoyed by two Italians playing - a street-organ before his house. Giving his ser- vant some money, he told her that whenever she heard an organ, she was to go out and pay the owners to take it away. This was a failure. The men, instead of coming once a week, came twice:

One day the sound of the organ disturbed the professor while working at a certain lecture. This so annoyed him that he rushe.d out an ordered the men away, telling them that if they came again he would hand them over to the police. They refused to go unless he gave them, more money. Enraged at their impertinence, he raced down the street in search of a police- man.

Just as he turned the corner of the street, he met a trgeant marching nine constables to, their beats. Without speaking, he turned and walked alongside the procession. When they turned the corner, the Italians saw the professor with the policemen. It was enough. They were both seized with a sudden desire to see how quickly they could get the organ out of the street. The cure was la-sting. for the professor declares•that no one has since been bold enougfi to play an organ before his house.

THE CANAL BCRST AT MARBURY.

; Two hundred men were engaged on Tuesday night in repairing the burst at the North Staffordshire Canal at Alarbury. The canal is being damned and clay brought from Anderton to restore the bed. Several weeks will elapse before communication is restored. The official measurements of the chasm are 76ft. by 60ft. and 2ft. deep.

CHORAL SOCIETY PICNIC.—On Saturday the members of the Great Sankey Choral Society had their annual trip, when they visited Matlock Bath. Warrington was left at 8.30 and on arrival at Matlock, short strolls and a little hill climEing were the otder until dinner was served at 12o'clock. Dinner over, the party indulged in whatever recleat ion took their fancy—mountaineering, boating, cave v'siting, and promenading. Warrington was again r« ached after ten o'clock.

div.head: Christian Creeds.
div.p: Christian Creeds.

Sir,—With your kind permission I should like to reply to a few points raised in your correspondence of Saturday last, in which a writer calling himself" Iosa" pleads for the reconciliation of the various conflicting Christian sects. Here in the beginning let me state that with the general subject of his letter dealing with secular education and the duties of Government, I am in complete agreement, but in the side issues we are widely divided. He alludes in the onset to one of these issues and regrets that the present divisions in the Christian ranks make it impossible for its adherents to come to any definite agreement. He states" that all' these proceed- ings are a scandal to a country calling itself Christian and arise from the melancholy fact that after 14 centuries of preaching we hay, not yet arrived at a common Christianity. I should like your correspondent to tell me why this should be, if the founder of Christianity really brought a divine revelation from the Infinite to the brain and heart of man? How is it that this revelation is so ambiguous that hundreds of conflicting sects have arisen, each claiming to be the only living truth, and hurling anathemas as every other. Surely where there is so much dissension, all should have the right to enquire the credentials of each, and having examined, hare the right to reject. I cheerfully admit there are many good things in the New Testament, and if we take from these books the dogmas of eternal pain, of infinite revenge; of the Atonement; of the necessity of shedding innocent blood ,• if we throw away the teach- ing of non-resistanoe ; of loving enemies ; that pros- perity is the result of wickedness ; that poverty is a preparation for Paradise ; there may remain sufficient base for a reasonable and decent religion. Your correspondent again states that the Gospel according to its Divine Founderand immediate followers is relegated to the background while the various sects formulated creeds of their own. But from where have these sects obtained their authority but from these very gospels to which he refers. Would not every sect from haughty Rome, down to the most insignificant few, meeting in two or threes in obscure corners, point to some passage within its pages endorsing their action and upholding their creed? Why did not Christ plainly say what views he held on human rights, on the sacred- ness of home, on the question of education, on the rights of investigation, on liberty and truth? Why did He not say which mode of baptism was pleasing to Him ; -why did He not write a creed Himself instead of leaving all He said or did to be told by others who might Con- trovert his meaning? I hold that wherever Christ did speak plainly his teachings are mainly impossible, while often they are vague,miSieading and absurd. I should like to ask your correspondent what new truth this Divine Founder brought to the world? So far I have failed to discover any. Did he bring a rule of conduct? The world's great philosophers had .don o this before he was born. "His new command- ment "was old in India long before. The real truth is Christian teachings no longer reach the highest level of human thought, nor satisfy thehungering aspirations of the heart. In vain men try to bring them forward on social questions only to end in deepest disappointments. No longer can these empty shibboleths, uttered by scheming priests into the wondering ear of faith, be believed in for a moment by the brain that has been touched and quickened by reason's guiding star. Our brains no longer sleep while droning priests chant forth their worse than useless creeds, but with eyes wide open we read with them the dusty page, and while our reason hold the scales, we weigh with calm unhiassed minds, the good and bad, the foolish and the wise, and try to find among the useless chaff,the golden grain that alone can zatisfy the hunger of the heart and brain of man.—Your truly, ALEC GRDISHAW.

div.head: Warrington Secular Society. An Ex-Warrington House-wife's Plaint.
div.p: Warrington Secular Society. An Ex-Warrington House-wife's Plaint.
Sir,--I have read with interest the letter in last

week's "Examiner," by "an Ex-Warrington House- wife" (happy she that she can write Ex "!) And would like to endorse and emphasize every word of it. I wonder every day that Warrington housewives have borne the horrible condition of things so long. They must be an exceedingly patient and long-suffering race, or is it that they have sunk into a hopeless state, and simply endure without hope of a cure? The battle with smoke and soot, and their consequences, is an incessant one, and leaves us poor women without time, strength, or spirit for anything higher or nobler than the scrubbing-brush and the wash-tab. Surely it was -never intended that our lives should be spent in such an ignoble warfare. We are so weary with the fight, body and brain alike fatigued, and the heart almost broken with the uselessness and hopelessness of it all, that when evening comes and husband and children have a right to expect brightness and cheerfulness, in the "house-mother," and an intelligent interest in their work and lesscns, their pleasuves and their griefs, it seems impossible to flog the tired spirt into activity, and the" little rift " opens and ever-widens, until in many a home the music has been slowly silenced. How impossible it is to attend to the mental and moral needs of our children, when the whole time and strength are absorbed in simply keeping home and clothes and persons clean (and lamentably failing even then) no one who has not tried it knows. And the physical health breaks down under the strain,aggravated and intensified as it is by the condition of the atmosphere, which chokes and clogs the lungs and skin, and, too often brings on a throbbing headache. Is it any wonder if the nerves give way under the strain and irritibility and bad, temper are the result ? And worst of all, when late at night one has dragged one's weary limbs up-stairs, one is sadly too often too tired for thought or prayer, and the inner life, unnourished and unfed, dwindles and dies, until one becomes little better than a machine, or one of the brutes that perish. Must it be always so? The clouds of smoke that almost incessantly poor out of the hunareds of large chimneys, are not surely a necessary adjunct to prosperity. As I was complaining one day of the dense masses which " thronged the air and darkened heaven" an old man said " Ah! it wor blacker when there wor none," and I certainly am not wishing for a return of that time. But I cannot believe that the present state of things is real economy. And if to make a change were costly—though I have heard that in a very few years the cost would be more than repaid by the reduc- tion in fuel—surely we have a right 'to ask from those in our town, that something may be done to relieve us of this incubus. For our children's sake, that they may have a chance of health inn purer air, of greater happi- ness and more mother-care, for the sake of our over- worked women, that some little leisure may be given them in their life of toil, and for the men's sake that it my be possible for them to find in their wives com- panions, and not simply drudges, I plead. Sunlight and pure air are God's gifts to all His creatures,— wherein have we forfeited our right to them ?—I am, sir, yours, &c.,
ONE WHO SUFFERS STILL.

Sir,—ln last weeks " Examiner," I saw a letter, from an ex-Warrington Ilady, who has been so fortunate, as to leave the dust and smoke of the town behind and dwell where the air is purer and cleaner. Is it not possible to, in some degree, lessen the amount of smoke and dust which we are at present compelled to tolerate. It is almost an impossibility, for the wife of the working man to keep her house, and children as spotless and clean as she would like. From early morning, until late at night, she must toil; so that not only are the neutral things of home, being worn out by the repeated rubbing and scouring they are subject to, but also the health and strength of the wife and mother,•

Did we know exactly the difference in the amount spent on renewing wash-worn articles, and in buying soap &c., between one family in the town and another in the country, I think it would surprise some of us to find how much of our husband's hard earned money goes in the fight to keep our homes sweet and clean, which under more favour- able conditions we could use to secure some little home comfort which we need, but which we cannot now afford. The vast amount of energy we are constantly usiag up in this way is more than should be necessary. Every one of us wants all the pleasure we can get out of life, we want to live and not merely exist, so if only something could be done to abate these evils that rob life of its brightness and joy, I am sure every working woman would be as thankful as myself.—Yours Sus., A WORKINGMAN'S WIFE.

div.head: EX-WARRINGTON HOUSEWIFE.
div.p: THE EX-WARRINGTON HOUSEWIFE.

We have heard of the Warrington housewife • Who from Warrington ran away; From the smoke and the smut and the smirches, Bat some of us have to stay. She has found a salubrious climate, Which bears of this carbm no stain. She has left all her sorrows behind her, But what about those who remain ? They run off as soon as they're able, To Latchford and Stockton Heath : From the heights of Hill Cliffe they look down on The Stygean vapours beneath.
The lucky ones leave it behind them, They think of it when they are gc•ne ; But the people that earn them the money, Working-man'and his wife must stay on.
She tells of the dirt on the curtains, The srnuts on the children's face, The pitiful state of their noses Within and without a disgrace.
The curtains will clean at the laundry The back kitchen laundry we know; The children's faces will polish, And even their noses also.

But what of the lungs of the children, The dirt that accumulates there ; Neither soap nor water will cleanse them Nor preserve their blood pure and fair. And what of the temper and spirit, Born down in the terrible strife ; The burden that others can flee from Presses hard on the working man's wife. Do you wm.der that men fill the publics And hurry from homes such as these; Where children have lost their bright faces And wives have forgotten to please. The children are dying by thousands, The wealth of the nation lies there ; They are perishing under the burden of the drink and the dirt —cursed pair. N.B.—Of the children born in Warrington 1.57 per thousand die under the twelvemonth.

div.head: WEDDING AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: WEDDING AT LATCHFORD.
Gibbs Longbottom.

Public interest was extensively aroused in Latchford .by the wedding which took place at Christ Church, Wash-lane, on Thursday. The contracting parties were Mr. Stanley Gibbs, s-m of Mr. H. IlGibbs, of Norfolk, and Nellie, daughter -of Mr. W. Longbottom, Latchford, a prominent and much respected officer of the Church. There was a large attendance both inside and outside the sacred building,and many regrets were expressed that the sun failed to grace the ceremony by his presence. The officiating clergymen were the Rev. Canon Willis, rector of Warrington and the Rev. G. C. Briggs, vicar of Christ Church. kiss Longbottom was attended at the altar by three bridesmaids, Miss Lilian Lomax (Huyton),Miss Nellie Longbottom (cousin, Sheffield), and Miss Kathleen Gibbs (sister of the bridegroom). The bride, who was given away by her father, was handsomely attired in a dress of ivory chiffon taffeta trimmed with embroidered chiffon; she wore an embroidered veil of Brussels net with wreath of orange blossom and carried a shower bouquet of anunciation lilies, stephanotis, white roses, lilies of the valley and maidenhair. Mrs. Longbottom, the bride's mother, wore a dress of dove grey marquisette trimmed with embroidered chiffon and touches of pink silk, with hat to match, and bouquet of sweet peas and lilies of the valley. The bridesmaids wore white book muslin semi-Empire frocks, trimmed with lace and pale blue ribbon, blue sashes, white crinoline French hats trimmed with white ostrich feathers shading to pale blue, and tulle, and carried bouquets of pink carna- tions tied with blue ribbon. The bridegroom's mother wore black satin and lace with tuscan toque and ostrich feathers. Mr. Ernest Longbottom, brother of the bride, acted as best man. The organist was Mr. T. S. Fry, who played "The voice that breath'd o'er Eden" and "0 perfect love." After the ceremony the wedding party was entertained at the home of the bride, Rose Dale, Marlboro' Crescent, a marquee being erected on the lawn. The newly- wedded pair are spending the honeymoon in North Wales, and Mrs. Gibbs travelled in a Hungarian blue cloth costume with cream braided vest, braided with black silk military braid,and wore a large leghorn hat trimmed blue with French roses and blue chins ribb Jn. div.head: GOLFERS AND TEIEIR RULES.
div.p: GOLFERS AND TEIEIR RULES.

With regard to the ball that is lost, there is no doubt that the inequality of the heavy penalty for such a loss as compared with the light penalty for driving out of bounds is not equitable ; but the rule was framed in its present form with a special object to avoid the loss of time occasioned by going back to play another ball, and the loss of temper which might arise if the rule per- mitted the dropping of another ball near where the other was supposed to be lost and the opposing sides could not agree as to where that spot should be.— "Country Life."
