THANK'S TO THE CHAIRMAN. Mr. HERBERT HATTON' proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding. He said in these days there was no more diNcult task than for any ram to stand up and account for the shrinkage of values of which they were tired of hearing, and to attempt to give some forecast of the future. This most difficult task their Chairman undertook each half-year, and it seemed every time to get more difficult. He could assure the Chair- man that the feeling at any rate of local shareholders was that so long as he presided over their affairs, the business of the Bank in these arduous times would continue successful. He hoped that Mr. Parr would be long spared to preside over those meetings And that they might live to see him rejoice in consols being once more restored. (Laughter.) LA.WSON seconded, and the resolution was very cordially passed. The CFUIRMAN thanked the meeting both on his own and on his fellow directors' behalf. He recognised the generous feelings of the sharebolders,and said if he took everything seriously he would grow quite conceited. He however, went back into the world and got this taken out of him again—(laughter)--and then Caine back with a renewed amount of modesty. (Renewed laughter.) The meeting then terminated.

div.head: CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL
div.p: CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL
Annual Meeting.
The annual meetink of the subscribers of the St. Elphin's Clergy Daughters' School was held on Darley Dale on Wednesday and was well attended. Mr. W. Shakerley presiding.

take in report A satisfactory report was presented upon the examina- i on of the 'school in chemistry, the theoretical work, said the examiner, reaching a high standard. The practical work was not up to the same standard. The Oxford Local examiner reported that in all subjects he found signs of thorough, conscien- tious and intelligent instruction. At no point did he detect weakness in method. At very many points he felt that a high standard had been aimed at. He was distinctly of opinion that the condition of the school was—to say the least—as satisfactory as it was a year ago, and that it was providing a sound education on broad modern lines.

Miss KENNEDY, the headmistress, presented her annual report, in which she showed that satisfactory progress was being made. The retiring members of the Committee of Aranage- ment were unanimously re-elected, whilst the Rev, W. R. Clayton (Manchester), Mr. J. Reads!! (Sale), and Mr. Richard A. de A"Nillis (Liverpool), were elected to fill three vacancies. The Revs. G. B. Thurston, W. J. Bradford and Canon Penrhyn, and Messrs. John White, Herbert S. Woodcock, and W. P. Fullagan were appointed representatives on the Board of Finance. COVINTITTEE OF MANAGENIENP'S REPORT.

Canon WILSON, of Worcester, presented the report of the Committee of Nlanagernent to the subscribers. It stated that throughout the period covered by the report —September, 1906-July, 1907—the health of the school, as a whole, had been very good, as might be expected from its position and arrangements. The conduct of the girls had been entirely satisfactory. The school was animated by a spirit of loyalty and industry and cheerful activity, due to the excellent Headmistress and her able and willing staff. The number of pupils was 79, of whom six were likely to leave at the end of the term. The number of applicants for admission was 15, and would probably soon be increased. They looked forward to there being about 90 in the school next term, and they could only be received by arranging that some of the mistresses should have rooms outside the school buildings. Further, the Board of Education in 1906 made it one of their copditions for continuing to recognise their training department for secondary teachers, that by the summer of 1909 the number of girls should be less than 100. These considera- tions forced on the Committee the question of providing an additional dormitory. The chapel, the dining hall, the class rooms, playing fields, sanatorium and gymnasium were sufncient for 120. It was therefore necessary, if the school was to be thus increased that both the capital sum required for the extension be given in donations,and that further endow- ment or subscriptions be provided to meet the increased demand for major bursariestand thus extend the benefits conferred by the school on the clergy of the three diooeses. The Training Department attached to St. Elphins was becoming well-known so that their student teachers were at once, and even before they left, offered good posts in secondary schools. The results of the examination in 1906, which wen the latest at hand when the report was written, were highly satifactory. The committee sanctioned the appointment a year ago of a resident mistress for teaching physical exercises, swimming, dancing, and games, and the experiment had certainly been successful. In conclusion the one point on which friends of the school should concentrate their energies was the increase of the endowment and sub- scription list for which an appeal will shortly be made public.

div.head: ALL BLACKS.
div.p: THE ALL BLACKS.
Will the Northern Union Scheme Drop Through?
NEW zELAND UNI ON'S STRONG MEASURES

--- The fohowing appeared in the "Evening Chronicle" last night :—Mr. C. Wray Palliser, who represents the New Zealand Rugby Union on this side does not hold out any hopes of the promised " All Blacks ' " tour under Northern Union rules being a success. "Perhaps I bad better tell you the history of this thing," said Mr. Palliser to a Sportsman " representa- tive. " When I knew definitely that the proposed tour was not merely idle newspaper gossip, but likely to take form, I wrote at once to the New Zaaland Union." "What has been done ?"

"The promoters went about their work very quietly and very secretly in New Zealand. They were well aware that if particulars of it leaked out before the proper time a storm of indignation and dissatisfaction would be aroused amongst all classes. " Directly the Union heard what was afoot they took immediate action. Players nominated for representa- tive honours were asked to make a declaration before a Justice of the Peace. The Union drew up a stringent form' which at first was signed by OS out of 70 representative first-class players. Of the two who did not sign one was a member of the late team that toured in Great Britain. Afterwards he reconsidered his position, and attached his signature. That is to say, 09 out of 70 of the crack Rugby footballers of New Zealand, the cream of the men now playing the game, have declared upon oath their allegiance to the New Zealand Union and its amateur principles. The sixty-nine are men picked by the eighteen District Unions as being worthy of, selec- tion for the great annual fixture, North Island v. South Island, which corresponds in importance to your Inter- national matchss.

"In order to make assurance doubly sure, the officials also secured an agreement from each of the 30 players who participated in that match. The agreement states (here follows name and address) 'will not form one of the projected team of footballers to play against the Northern Union of England.' "To English ideas," continued the Colonial," these precautions may sound very peculiar, but it must be remembered that the New Zealand U,rion have been fighting an unknown enemy; an enemy who was only waiting for the best men to be picked not only for the North Island v. South Island nut also for the approach- ing New Zealand Union tour in Australia, in order that their own task of selection might be made from the best available talents That, however, has now been defeated. The promoter of this projected visit has been identified. He is a player, but not of the first class. He has been suspended under the professional laws and warned off all grounds in the Colony. "From what I have told you, coupled with other information that has come to my knowledge,' I think there is little fear of this New Zealand professional team reaching Northern Union groend. But if by some chance a team of sorts should venture upon a trip, it will, I am convinced, be sadly disappointing to all con- cerned in it. Financially, I should say any undertaking of thia kind would result in failure." " Do you think any of the players who were here in 1905 are likely to come again as professionals ?"—" No, I feel certain they will not." Notwithstanding the alarmist report quoted above, we do not conclude that the prospects of a strong New Zealand team visiting the Northern Union are remote. The arrangements have been in hand for a considerable time, and so assured are the Northern Union managers that the fixture list for the visitors has been made up. No secret has been made of the fact that the names of the visiting players are known to the officials, who consider them a sufficient guarantee of the strength of the New Zealand team.

div.head: Canon Gibson Smith Advocates a Native System.
div.p: Canon Gibson Smith Advocates a Native System.

Thursday was Speech Day at the Grammar School and the time honoured event was attended with all due ceremony. There was however over all an air of sadness at the absence through illness of the popular headmaster the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, whose cheery face and commanding figure were keenly missed. As in the past the proceedings took place in the large schoolroom which was specially decorated for the occasion,and by the students of the school in particular was the greatest enthusiasm displayed. The Rev, J. Forbes, lleathlield, Latchford, presided over a large and fashionable gathering, being supported by Canon Gibson Smith of Liverpool, whose duty it was to hand the book prizes and certificates to the success- ful students. At the conclusion of the prize giving the scholars proceeded to entertain the guests, plays in French, Greek and English being presented. All the boys acted well and their efforts were highly appre- ciated. The plays together with dramatis personae. were :

The CHAIRMAN said he was sure all present would share in the regret at the Headmaster not being able to be present that afternoon. He would like to express on behalf of Mr. Willcocks his appreciation of the excep- tionally devoted and faithful service his colleagues had rendered to him during the past months. They had to bear their share of the burden which had fallen upon the headmaster and he would like to say how very deeply Mr. Willcocks appreciated their devotion. If the head- master was not able to be present in body that afternoon he was there in spirit and mind. The keenness of the interest which Mr. Willcocks had taken in that day's proceedings as well as in the examinations was extra- ordinary when one came to remember the suffering he had had to undergo. It had been his mind which had guided, his will which had dominated; he may not have been their in body, he had been there in mind. One thing which he (the speaker) wished to take back with him was that that day's proceedings had been no less successful than any of previous years. He thought the headmaster had a great deal to be proud of when two of his old colleagues Canon Gibson-Smith and himself were there that afternoon and it was the very best testimonial they could give to the school that the head- master could not only train the boys and win their respect but could also train the masters and win their respect and devotion. (Applause.) Canon GIBSON SMITH said it was with no little emotion that he rose to address them in that once familiar school. Twenty-six years had passed away since he first entered that school a raw recruit in the warefare of life with much to learn, many mistakes to make and much kindnesss' consideration and forbear- ance to receive both from the pupils,from his colleagues and above all from the headmaster with whom it was his hippy lot to work for ten years. He was sure they would all echo what had been said about the absence of Mr. Willcocks. (Hear, hear.) He had always found him a man of transparent goodness, generous forebear- ing, minutely painstaking, entirely filled with zeal for his work. In fact, his devotion to his work was splendid and he (the speaker) could say without the slightest exaggeration that during the ten years he knew Mr. Willcocks the cause of education and the cause of the school was not entirely absent from his mind for one hour of his waking life. (Applause.) Since that day a good deal of water had flowed under Warrington Bridge and as he grew older there was one maxim which impressed itself upon him more and more and that was that they learnt by teaching. Mark Patterson,late head of Lincoln College, perhaps in his day the most learned man in Europe, once said that when he wanted to learn anything thoroughly he would sit down and write a book about it. They learnt by teaching—learnt not only the facts, principles and methods but the strong and weak points of the human mind. It was true the power of teaching was a gift but it was a gift which had to be developed by exercise and in that they were in danger of being misled just now by the cry for the training of teachers especially of secondary teachers. Those who uttered that cry often fell into the mistake of enthusiasts, that was the mistake of exaggeration. Far be it from him to deny the value of training. Training could do much but it had its limits. There were certain things It could not do and which they must not expect it to do. For instance there was that subtle communion, heart with heart which must exist between the teacher and the taught, if the teaching was to be successful, which they called sympathy. No amount of training could give them that sympathy and yet without it there was little real education. It was said of a great headmaster that he had no method, no system, no technical skill and yet his boys were devoted to him and always did well both at the university and in after life. The secret of his success was that he had a great mind and a great heart. One of his old boys said that the boys felt they were in contact with a great mind and brought their whole powers to bear and taught themselves. That was the ideal of teaching, to persuade the pupils to teach themselves. There was a multiplex murmur, sometimes melodious,sornetimes strident,going through the land at the present time crying education ! education ! What was education ? To many it meant some parcel in the mind crammed with information packed as tight as it could be, which would enable the Englishman to beat the German and American in the race for wealth. To others it meant matured strength of a developed mind and a developed character which would enable the Englishman to play a man's part, to grapple with any emergency in life. The late Arch-Bishop Temple once said that a strong man would be required for a certain important post and asked, what he meant by "strong man" he replied a man who would always rise to the occasion in whatever situation he was placed. That was what he would use as the definition of an educated man. (Applause.) The value and power of education did not lie in the stores of knowledge which were acquired so much as in the habits a man acquired, in his intellectual energy, moral power, self conttol and resolute subdugation of the bony to the mind. That he thought was the reason why some of those who never won a prize at school sometimes gained the best prizes in after life. (Applause.) He was speaking of education in its widest sense and he included the school games as a part and a valuable part of the curriculum ; a part which our foreign competitors regarded with anxious envy. The famous remark that Waterloo was won on the playing fields of Eaton might be greatly extended and expanded to-day. School games gave the English- men character, that bonhomie and spirit of adventure and enterprise, that love of fair play and cold-blooded justice which had enabled him to take up the white man's burden and become the great colonizing power of the world, the great promoter of Christian civilization on earth. (Applause.) If games were an important part of education they were far from being the whole. If other nations had much to learn from us in the matter of school athletics we had much to learn from them in other departments. It was perhaps not surprising that a nation which was descended from the old sea dogs, which had enterprise as to its great characteristic should not be distinguished for the patience, quiet persistence, love of method, minute perfection in detail which were the main features of the German character. He asked "could the leopard change its spots? Could the English pioneer become the German plodder ?" He doubted it, and be doubted further whether German or any other foreign system of educa- tion would serve to develop it and therefore we must have a native system adopted to our native needs. No amount of training, foreign or otherwise would turn a shire horse into a hackney, or make a race horse a success at drawing a plough. The German nation had its own peculiar characteristics and so had the English, and the educational system which would serve admir- ably for one was not by that means adapted for the other. Matthew Arnold spoke of the German educa- tion chiefly for two things. Firstly the Germans believed in it. The great mass of. the English people , did not believe in education as the German did and until the people of this country began to do so education would make but poor progress amongst us. Many thought they could obtain education by legisla- tion but the English people could not and would not be driven. They might be led but they would not be driven and that was where politicians very often went wrong. The second point in the German system,was the wonderful organization. The English as a race had not the gift for organization and whilst they admired it so much in others it was not in their blood. What department of the English State was thoroughly organized? The late Boer War brought the fact home, we were not prepared. Were we ever prepared? The question therefore was could we learn organization? Within certain limits he believed any

race of men could learn anything just as an any individual could. (Hear, hear.) Were they right in , thinking that the German system of education was the' beat possible for the German? They were not all unanimous on the point in Germany. Some were even kind enough to think there was something for them to learn in England in the matter of education. One who knew Germany and England equally well—Sir Ellis Barker—said the results of German education were not superior to those of Groat Britain from the point of view of national utility. As to the real causes of German prosperity, Sir Ellis urged two things, first the German character was amenable to discipline and where individuals could sub-ordinate their interest to the common good the whole community was bound to prosper His second point was the assiduity of the Germans and their willingness to work. It was said of the people of England that they preferred to get the work done for them. It had even been said that an English cross- ing sweeper would be an employer of labour if he could get anyone to labour for him. Life itself was the great educator and they found as time went on that character was more important than attainments. As Solomon said " Wisdom (meaning character) is the principal thing therefore get wisdom and with all that get good understanding." (Applause.) In his annual report the HEADMASTER said the history of the school for the past twelve months con- tained nothing senstaional but was a record of much quiet honest work, patiently carried through to a suc- cessful issue. He was glad once again to testify publicly to the excellent qualifications of their teaching staff. Last par the results of the Oxford Local Examination were exceedingly satisfactory. Out of 19 candidates who obtained certificates 15 were placed in the honours division and four were specially distinguished in various subjects. The list was in one respect a record one, as all the candidates eligible for honours obtained them. The successes were four first classes, five second classes, six third classes and four passes over age. All their senior candidates were excused the London matricula- tion examination and also the joint matriculation examination of Liverpool and Manchester Universities. Three were excused responsions in stated subjects at Oxford. The results for the present year were not pub- lished, but the examiner of the school, Mr. C. H. Sampson, said that on the examination as a whole he would unreservedly congratulate the school. Colitinu- ing, Mr. Sampson said, I was shown the whole of the school buildings and their general equipment. The improvement in this respect is most striking and most satisfactory. The school appears to be now for its size as well equipped as it is staffed. The marked feature of the work in Form VI. is the extra- ordinary viideness of the curriculum. Not only in classics and mathematics, but in English literature English and Roman history and political economy remarkable success is achieved. The all-round excel- lence of Form V. is beyond praise. The results in - Latin are excellent not only in the case of boys on the classical side but in several instances in the case of boys on the modern side. The same praise is due to the Greek on the classical side of this Form and also to the German on the modern side. In mathematical subjects I look forward with special interest to the work that I may be done in the future by some boys of marked ability when they pass cn to higher work. Among the junior boys there is much promising material in the second form. I was fully satisfied with the Algebra and geometry of the third Form. The teaching of , French appears to me admirable throughout the school." Among the list of successes which were to be announced were, H. Dutton exhibition of the value of ..-C3O per annum at St. John's College, Cambridge, P. Kennon, Ist class in the matriculation examination of Liverpool University and qualified for the Gee scholar- ship which he was not able to hold as he had already obtained a Tate scholarship of £35 per annum; H, Nield 2nd class in the matriculation e,camination of I Liverpool University; H. 0. Adams, R. Lee, R. Wilcox , are excused responsions in stated subjects at Oxford; 'H. 0. Adams, R. Lee, R. Wilcox, and A. Wright are excused the London matriculation examination and also the joint matriculation examination of the uni- versities of Liverpool and Manchester ' • J. Bamforth has passed let M. 8., Ch.B. of Liverpool University; W. Greene has oh ained his B.A. at London University; 0. H. Cooke has passed his final examination for admis- sion to the Bar; C. T. Cooke has passed the London L.L.B. examination of London University; G. W. Joseph has passed the final examination with honours for the degree of M. 8., Ch.B. of Liverpool University; F. Carlisle passed the intermediate examination of the Incorporated Law Society; B. McGart3, passed the matriculation examination of the London University ; H. D. Johnson, passed the final examination for the Associateship of the Institute of Surveyors • J. R. Alderson, 2nd place in all England in the intermediate examination of the Institute of Chartered Accountants ; R. Kennon and H. Nield, passed the first examination for the degree of M. 8., Ch. 8., Liverpool University. Continuing, Mr. WILLCOCKS said the advance in educational ideals made advance in structural efficiency imperative, and almost a revolution had been worked in their housing. The scheme of the work had been re-modelled and the forms re-organized so that they satisfied the most stringent demands of that somewhat arbitrary and autocratic body the Board of Educa- tion. The new scheme of the Board under Which the school was governed was now fully at work. They had an increasing number of boys, and every sign pointed to a contivation of the old tradition so long and happily assdciated with the school —a sound and a liberal education. (Applause). div.head: PARR'S BANK, LIMITED.
div.p: PARR'S BANK, LIMITED.
HALF-YEARLY MEETING.

An extraordinary general meeting of Parr's Bank, Limited, was held at the Bank Premises,Winwick-street, on Thursday at noon. Mr. Cecil F. Parr, chairman of directors, presided, and the following directors were also present :—Nlessrs. Thomas A. Dixon, John Dunn, N. Farrington Eckersly, Alfred Hewlett, Robert Neill, and A. Morrison Turner : also Mr. R. W. Whalley, general manager ; 'fr. E. D. Hyatt, secretary, and a number of shareholders.

div.head: DEATH OF SIR DAVID GA\IBLE.
div.p: THE DEATH OF SIR DAVID GA\IBLE.

The CHAERMAN said before proceeding with his general remarks, he must refer to the death and express their very great regret—their unanimous regret—At the death of Sir David Gamble. This took place some months ago, but to those present, especially to those who belonged to Lancaahire,it was as fresh as though it happened yesterday. (Hear, hear). Sir David was a member of that Board from the very inception of the Bank as a limited company, and from that day forth he had watched over the Bank's interest, and had been concerned in its development into the very important institution it had now become. Though travelling to London invnlved to him, in view of his advancing years great personal sacrifice, still up to the very end, or almost to the very end, he attended regularly at the London Board and 'crave them his best advice. No man on the Board had akeener sense of his duty to the Bank, and no man had a more earnest desire to serve it. He was sure that every shareholder owed a great debt of gratitude to Sir David for the very great services and the wide experience of men and matters he was able to bring to the benefit of the Board. (Hear, hear.) It was with very great pleasure he was able to tell them that his son Sir Christopher had consented to fill his father's place at their Board, and the shareholders would be asked that day to confirm that election. DEATH OF A LOCAL DIRECTOR.

Mr. PARR said the Bank had also to deplore the loss by death of one of their local directors at Leicester,Mr. Baines whose high character and position of great influence in his native town was very useful to them in Leicester.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF VICE-CHAIRNIA)T.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF VICE-CHAIRNIA)T.

The CHAIRMAN informed the meeting that Mr. Nix, who had done a very great deal of good work for the Bank in his position of vice-chairman for some years, had asked to be relieved from his responsibilities, and Mr. A. J. Frazer, whose knowledge of the City, and whose experieace of the City, was almost unique and unequalled, had kindly consented to assume those responsibilities and was now their Deputy-Chairman.
CHAIRMAN'S ADDRESS. THE PRICE OF CONSOLS.

The CHAIRMAN said one was tired almost of hearing the question" What is it that makes consols so low ? " Among other answers given were political disturbances and unrest abroad, the policy and actions of borne Government, the new social forces, or the perpetually impending new issues. All those issues had been brought forward to account for this drop. Doubtless all these causes had had an effect in that way, but to his mind they were not sufficient to account for the gradual fall which had begun some years back, and bad continued with but little interruption to the present time. There was stock which, in the estimation of the public, was almost considered as gilt-edged as consols themselves, and yet which, broadly .speaking, was unaffected by any of the above causes which he had enumerated, which tended to influence the consol market. There was an investment which was unmoved by political crisis or by cross currents of speculation, or even by the fierce winds of commercial crisis. That was the stock of the Bank of England. The Bank of England stock still held its own, and rightly held its own in the esteem and confidence of the public, but that stock had fallen very considerably more in pro- portion and relatively than consols. He ventured to point out some years ago that there was another reason which from its very simplicity was apt to be overlooked, and that was that the investing public were no longer content with a 3 per cent. return,for it must be remembered that 21 per cent.at the price 83:! returned just as much as consols at 3 per cent.did when they were very widely bought some years ago at 100. The genuine investor had discovered some really safe investments which would return at least 31, per cent.—an extra per cent.—and this feeling was reflected, as they knew, in modern trust deed settlements, for which there was much greater latitude given than was formerly the case. Naturally trustees in these cases did their best for the beneficiaries within the legal limits of their trusts. In ' former days, banks and insurance companies were large and steady purchasers of consols. They continued to hold a very large amount which they had years ago, and in his opinion they held them rightly, bur in late years, he did not think they had very largely increased their holdings. So this really came to the old law of supply and demand, and the price of consols had fallen away from lack of purchasers. THE JAPANESE WAR. During the last half year, through the help of their good friends, the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, the Yokohama Specie Bank, and Messrs. Rothschild, Mr. Whalley had been able to carry through negotiations with his usual tact and ability for the con Ter sion of a loan for the Japanese Government. That was perhaps a more than usually difficult and delicate operation, when they considered the very awk ward conditions which prevailed up to the very moment of issue. Therefore very great credit was due to those who were responsible for the success, which it undoubtedly was.

div.head: THE. MANCHURIAN RAILWAY LOAN.
div.p: THE. MANCHURIAN RAILWAY LOAN.

Some present would have noticed that they had been interested with the above-named banks in the issue of the Manchurian Railway Loan. This also had the guarantee of the Japanese Government, and therefore was as good a security as a direct loan to the Government. In this instance the three banks acted as agents for the Industrial Bank of Japan. In tho present condition of the money market, he thought they were very fortunate that the loan had been applied for so ext3nsively as it had been.

BANK ITEMS. The shareholders would observe in the balance sheet that they had written down one million consols •at 83. He need hardly say that this was merely a recognition of the elementary fact that what had happened once might easily happen again. He confessed he had some- times wondered why on their balance-sheet they had not placed all their different securities together, for those million consols were not all they possessed. They held considerably more than a million, and the rest had also been written down at 83. The rest were placed under the item " British Government Securities." Therefore if some day those million consols disappeared from the balance sheet (laughter), he hoped it would not be regarded as a startling and dangerous innovation. They were placing £15,000 to their premises account instead of their usual £lO,OOO. He might here mention that with regard to the latest Compensation Act, which they knew to their cost, they were doing their own insuring in respect of all their clerks who were receiving less than £250 per annum. He did not think there were any other items in the balance sheet which needed special remark. They were all good. Cash in haad and money at call, they would notice was 3.3 per cent, of the whole liabilities to the public. The shareholders had increased in numbers, their customers had increased in numbers and their deposits had increased. The price of their shares had fluctuated during the last few months from 84 to 88. In view of very free criticism during the past year of certain organs of the press which had attacked banks both in London and the country, he thought it was very satisfactory that in view of the very heavy depreciation of securities, in no single instance, had they dropped their dividend. (Hear, hear.) That was substantial evidence of solidity and the appreciation of the investing public. In the case of more than twenty banks, their securities had gone up from to as much as 21 points. Trade on the whole continued good, and there were good signs that it would continue good for some time. The Stock Exchange, he was afraid, was still in doldrums. waiting for a favourable breeze of investment and , speculation. Mr. Parr then proceeded to refer briefly ! to a pending action against a Society paper in which ; the Bank had engaged Mr. Rufus Isaacs as their counsel, and in conclusion he moved that the report and balance sheet be adopted and a half year's dividend of 19 per cent. per annum free of income tax payable on August let be passed. Mr. DrxoN seconded. Mr. LAWSON wished to know how much the Bank premises account and the officers' pension fund amounted to at the present time. The CHAIRMAN said the bank premises account amounted to £825,649 4s. 2d. which was considerably less than the premises were worth in the estimation of directors. The officers' pension fund amounted to £90,000. The resolution was adopted. • i NEW DIRECTOR. On the .motion of the Orr tram tx seconded by Mr. NEILL. Sir Christopher Gamble, Bart., was elected a director of the company.

AUGUST BANE: HOLIDAY ON THE CONTINENT. Tickets at reduced fares available for eight days will be issued to Brussels July 31st August Ist, 2nd, 3rd and sth,and to Zurich via Harwich and Antwerp. Passengers leaving the Northern or Midland Counties in the after- noon reach Brussels next morning after a comfortable night's rest on board the steamer. For visiting The Hague, Scheveningen (The Dutch Brighton) and Amsterdam for the desd Cities of the Zuyder Zee, special facilities are offered via the Great Eastern Rail- way Company's British Royal Mail Harwich-Hook of Holland route. From the Hook of Holland through carriages and restaurant cars are run in the North and South German Express trains to Cologne, Bale and Berlin,reaching Cologne at noon, Bale and Berlin in the evening. L. & N.-W. RAILWAY TRIPS.

We would refer our readers to our advertising column in which will be found the advertisement of the special cheap trips arranged by the L. and N.-W. Railway Company. An is their usual custom they have again a large and varied list of cheap trips to suit all classes, and to some of the principal ones we would draw atten- tion. On August 2 and 1 special excursion trains will run to London (Piston), and on the Ist and Bth to all parts of Scotland, by the Royal Mail route, via the West Coast. To the West of England, and Eastern Counties on the 2nd. On the 2,3, and sth to the South Coast watering places. On the 2nd and 3rd to Dublin and Interior stations in Ireland, by the short sea route via Holyhead. To York, Durham, and the North Eastern Line on the 3rd, and to Huddersfield, Dewsbury and Leeds on the 3 and sth. On August 2, 3 and sth to the North Wales Line, and on the 2nd to South and Central Wales. Numerous other excursions have been arranged to Wolverhampton, Birmingham, Blackpool, Manchester and Liverpool. In addition to the special facilities which are announced, the week-end tickets is:med on Friday and Saturday will be available to return on Sunday (train service permitting), Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

THIS COMPANY has been formed for the purpose of purchasing or acquiring on lease suitable estates or plots of land in. or on the immediate outskirts of the town of Warringtnn, with the intention of establishing GARDEN SUBURBS in order to provide the inhabitants of the town and neighbourhood with convenient, healthy and attractive residences at moderate rentals. The conditions surrounding the houses and homes of the people are vital to the well- being of the nation, and the movement which is rapidly spreading over linglend for the establishment of GARDEN CITIES AND SUBURBS indicates a way by which, through the voluntary association of all classes, much may be done on practical and business lines to solve a difficult problem. The ' desire of the promoters is to localize the methods which have been successful in other places with a view to improving Ithe conditions under which many of the working people of Warrington at present have to live. EACH ESTATE will be carefully selected with due regard to accessibility. appearance, health, arid economy of build- ing, and laid out as a whole under the best available expert advice. By adopting comprehensive methods of develop- ment in all their estates the promoters confidently anticipate that they will be able to effect substantial economies and to avoid much of the waste which is incidental to indivielual building and, at the same time, to make it possible for each suburb to have Its own characteristics, the buildings to be planned and arranged with reference to the beauty and convenience of the whole. The houses may be erected either by the Company, or by subsidiary Companies or Societies, or by both, or by private enterprise, the Company retaining the freehold, where such estate is vested in it, the ground rents which will be created being available for the payment of the Company's working expenses and fixed dividends, Preliminary steps have already been taken with a view to the formation of co-operative 9;enente Societies to assist in the experiment on the lines which have proved so successful at Baling and in other places, and it is hoped that one or more of these will be registered very shortly. FUNDA- MENTAL FEATURES of the scheme are that ample provision shall be made for open spaces for ornamental or recreative purposes, that each house shall have a garden, that not more than a certain specified nismber of houses per afire shall be erected, and that all plans shall be subject to the approval of tiae Company. NEGOTIATIONS are well advanced for the purchase of two sites, one at Great Sankey and she other at Grappenhali, The former is situated within ten minutes' walk of the Cor- poration Tram Service. It contains about 20 acres of undulat- ing land, with good roads on two sides. The owners are the Governors of the Warrington Grammar School, and the price agreed to be paid is £225 per acre (see plan enclosed). Mr. Bennett, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. Long, Mr. Parr, Mr. Roberts and Mr. Ryland', six of the Directors, !are Governors of the Grammar School, but they have no personal pecaniary Interest in the proposed sale. The Grappenhall site, known as Morris Brook Farm, contains about 2.? acre.. The owner Is Mrs. Mary Anne Bostock. of Kingsbridge. Devonshire, and the price agreed to be paid is £2.950. The land is close to Latchford Locks, on the Cheshire side, and in immediate proximity to several large works. Both sites are most suit- able for the Company's purposes, and, if they are acquired, the Directors intend to proceed as quickly Is possible with the promotion of Garden Suburbs thereon. No promotion money is being or has has been paid. A copy of the Memorandum and Articles of Association can be Inspected at the offices of the &Bettors to the Company at any time during business hours. A oopy of the Memorandum is printed at the end of this Prospect's, and forms part of it. The Articles if Association of the Company provide, as regards the qualification of the Directors, as follows : "84. Until otherwise determined by a General Meeting, the number of the Directors shall not be less than 5 nor more than 15. The qualification ot a Director shall he the holding in his own name in the Company's books shares of the Company of the nominal value of £lO on which all calls for the time being made have been paid. " 86. The Directors shall be paid out of the funds of the Company by way of remuneration for their services such sum as the Company in General Meeting may from time to time determine and such sum shall be , divided among the Directors in such proportion and manner as the Directors may determine." It may be added that the Directors have already promised to take up over £3,000 in shares. The minimum subscription upon which the Directors will proceed to alotment has been fixed at £5,000. The preli- minary expenses of and Incident to the formation and float- ing of the Company down to the time when it becomes entitled to commence business will be paid by the Company, and are estimated at £250. Application for shares should be made unon the accompany- ing form, and sent to the Bankers of the Company. The Manchester and Llverpeol District Banking Company, Limited, Sankey-street, Warrington, together with remit- tances for the amount payable on application. Prospectuses and forms of application can be obtained at the Registered Office of the Company, or from the Solicitors or Bankers. Dated 13th, July. 1907. THE RETURN ON THE SHARES will be limited to a ebruulstise dividend of Five Pounds per ceut. per annum. All surplus protits,after meeting the expenses of man.l4.rnetit and development, sul•jeet to the recommendati.ms of the Director,. will be applied eit h-r in the improvement of the Company's properties or in the extension of the scheme in other directions. None of the chases of this issue are being or have been issued otherwise than for cash. No commission has been paid or is payable for the sub- scription or underwriting of any Shares of this Ilene.

PRIMROSE LEAGUERS AT GRAPPENHALL HEYES• By the kind permission of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, the ruling councillor, the members of the Grappenhall Habitation (1,573) of the the Primrose League held their annual fete at Grappenhall Heyes, on Saturday, Charming weather prevailed and some 300 were present. The inspection of the gardens, conservatories, and fernery afforded much pleasure. Fishing was also per- mitted, and prizes were subsequently given to those catching the heaviest weights. The Pioneer Band was in attendance and discoursed excellent selections of music in the afternoon,and in the evening played for dancing. One of the most interesting features of the day's proceedings was the sports, which took place in one of the fields on the estate, the Sports Committee consisting of Messrs. H. Davenport, W. Mclntyre, Leyland, Robbins, Howard, Timperley, Ashcroft, Norbury, Taylor and T. Hankey. The judges were Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins, Lowe and Ashcroft, the starter Mr. Walter Howard, the handicappers for the cycle race Messrs. %V. Howard, W. A. Timperley and H. Daveiiport and the judges Messrs. Robbins, Davenport and elaidlaw. Money prizes were distributed to the successsful competitors by Mrs. Parr, the winners being as follow:- 110 Yards Flat Race.-1, W. Mclntyre; 2, F. Mclntyre ;;3, F. Parr. High Jump.—l, W. Mclntyre : 2, Walter Howard. Fishing Competition.-1, W. Gleave ; 2, J. L. Smith ; 3, Spencer. An excelleat tea was provided in a large rnarcr:ee, and the, catering of Mr. S. J. Woodcock gate great satisfaction. At the conclusion of the sports a short meeting in accordance with custom was held on the steps in front of the entrance to the house. Mr. Parr said that on a previous occasion he had to remind them that a very untoward circumstance had arisen which be said he hoped would be reversed at the first opportunity. They were caught napping at the latt election, but be hoped alley would never ho caught in that state again. (Hear, hear.') If be knew the men of Stockton Heath, Latch- ford, Grappenhall and other places be felt sure they would he more wide awake in future and that they would know what they had to do and.ahe determined to do it. They felt that things were not as they should be, and that the sooner they could put them right the better. (Applause.) Mr. AlcDermid proposed a vote of thanks to the officers, r,nd especially to the secretary, Miss Parr, for her excellent arrangements. Councillor Wilson seconded, and the motion was carried with great heartiness. A vote- of thanks was accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Parr on the motion of Mr. Jenkins seconded by Mr. Duckworth.
